records.statement: Where more information about originality is needed, the School may arrange an Exploratory Interview to check understanding. scope.audience: students

evidence.quote:
32.12 In such cases, the School may arrange an Exploratory Interview with the student in order to assess their understanding of the work they have submitted. The student will be asked questions about how they have undertaken their work by academic staff members familiar with the topic. If the student satisfies the School that they have produced the work, the work will be marked as normal. If concerns remain, the process below will be followed (for undergraduate non-Honours cases that are first breaches) or the case will be referred to the Student Conduct Team (for Honours, postgraduate and repeat cases). The notes from the Exploratory Interview should be included in any referral.
32.13 Normally, the student is expected to be unaccompanied, however they may request to be accompanied by a supporter. The accompanying individual can be a family member, another student or friend, or a member of University staff. This individual must not assist the student in answering questions about their work.

32.3 Students must not use generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools or AI-powered websites in ways which breach assessment instructions, for example to generate content, answers, or references. This applies to both individual and group assignments. Schools will advise students of their specific rules and in assessment specifications, where appropriate. Where the use of AI is permitted, it must be verified and appropriately referenced in the work for transparency, with details of how it was used being provided.

records.statement: Academic student-conduct appeals must use the prescribed form, state grounds and desired outcome, and be submitted in writing within ten working days of the date of the original-decision letter. Competent grounds are previously unavailable material evidence, materially detrimental procedural failure or a clearly unreasonable finding or sanction; this is distinct from the non-academic intention-to-appeal route.

scope.audience: students
qualifiers: Code33 Student Conduct; academic appeal route kept distinct from non-academic route

evidence.quote:
33.109 A Responding Student may appeal to the Senate Student Conduct Appeal Committee (the ‘Committee’) against a decision or sanction imposed by the Senate Assessors (in cases of academic misconduct), the Head of Student Conduct (in cases of non-academic misconduct), the Senate Student Academic Conduct Committee or the Senate Student Non-Academic Conduct Committee.
33.110 The Committee will consider an appeal only on the following grounds:
a) the Responding Student has new material evidence[11] that they were unable, for valid reasons, to provide earlier in the process and which is likely to have had a material bearing on a decision at the earlier stage;
b) the procedures set out in this Code have not been followed, to the material detriment of the Responding Student;
c) the finding of misconduct or sanction(s) imposed at the earlier stage was clearly unreasonable.
Appeal Against Academic Student Conduct Decisions
33.111 A Responding Student shall appeal in writing to student-conduct@glasgow.ac.uk for the attention of the Head of Student Conduct within 10 working days[7] of the date of the letter advising of the original decision.
33.112 The Student Conduct Appeal Form must be used to submit an appeal. The grounds of appeal must be clearly stated, detailing any new evidence (and why this could not have reasonably been produced at the earlier stage); describing how the procedure was defective; and/or explaining why the outcome was unreasonable. The outcome the Responding Student seeks must also be stated.

33.114 If an appeal is deemed by the Clerk of Senate (or nominee) and member of the Senate Student Academic Conduct Committee not to have met any of the grounds for appeal, or is out of time, the appeal will not be taken forward.
33.115 If an appeal is deemed by the Clerk of Senate (or nominee) and member of the Senate Student Academic Conduct Committee to have met one or more competent grounds for appeal, the appeal will be taken forward to a full hearing.

33.117 A Responding Student shall submit an appeal or intention to appeal in writing to student-conduct@glasgow.ac.uk for the attention of the Head of Student Conduct within 10 working days[7] of the date of the intimation of the original decision against which the student is appealing. Where an intention to appeal is submitted, the full appeal, including the grounds, remedy and all supporting evidence, shall be submitted within 20 working days of the student's intention to appeal submission.

records.statement: For 2026/27 supervised assessments, GenAI is generally not permitted unless the course coordinator expressly permits it in the assessment brief. Preparation or revision may use GenAI and does not require acknowledgement for these assessments. The restriction also covers AI-capable wearables.

scope.audience: students
qualifiers: Current 2026/27 guidance and Code 32; older published claims are a separately dated record. Assessments set under earlier rules retain their applicable instructions.

evidence.quote:
Scenario 1: For supervised assessments
Students are generally not permitted to use GenAI in supervised tasks unless the course coordinator has given express permission in the assessment brief. Students are able to use GenAI to undertake preparation or revision for these forms of assessment, but should be cognisant of over-reliance on GenAI tools undermining their independent thinking and learning.
This applies to:
In-person written examinations
in-class tests and quizzes
supervised practical work
oral presentations and vivas
any other assessment conducted under controlled conditions.
This restriction extends to wearable devices and other emerging technologies with AI capabilities. Using GenAI when it is not permitted constitutes a breach of academic integrity, but students do not need to reference/acknowledge the use of GenAI for preparation of/revision for these assessments.

localSummary.zh: 2026/27 监督评估一般不允许 GenAI，除非课程负责人在评估说明中明确许可；限制也涵盖具备 AI 能力的可穿戴设备。为这些评估进行准备或复习可以使用 GenAI，且不要求披露该准备或复习用途。

records.statement: For most 2026/27 unsupervised coursework or take-home assessments, GenAI may be used with acknowledgement, accuracy checks and substantially original work. A silent brief defaults to permission with acknowledgement, but course coordinators may restrict or prohibit use for a particular assessment. Submitting substantial GenAI work as your own and/or without acknowledgement remains misconduct.

scope.audience: students
qualifiers: Current 2026/27 guidance and Code 32; older published claims are a separately dated record. Assessments set under earlier rules retain their applicable instructions.

evidence.quote:
Scenario 2: For unsupervised assessment
For most coursework and take-home assessments, students may use GenAI tools provided they:
Acknowledge their use – explain what tools were used and how
Ensure the work remains substantially their own – GenAI should assist, not replace, original, independent thinking and learning
Verify accuracy – check all information, citations, and claims
Follow any specific instructions – course coordinators may set additional requirements or restrictions.
Course coordinators will specify, on an assessment by assessment basis, whether any limitations apply for the usage of AI within that assessment (including if AI must be used in only particular ways or, indeed, if AI use is not permitted at all). Where the brief is silent, the default position is that GenAI use is permitted with acknowledgement.
Course coordinators should set the expectation and tone that where students feel uncertainty about how GenAI can be used in a specific assessment, they should always ask in advance, rather than risk an unintentional breach of academic integrity.
Important: Students generating content with GenAI and submitting it as if it were their own work – without acknowledgement and/or when the GenAI contribution is substantial – is academic misconduct, regardless of whether the assessment is supervised or unsupervised.

localSummary.zh: 2026/27 大多数非监督作业或居家评估允许在披露、核实准确性且作品实质上由本人完成的条件下使用 GenAI。说明未提及 AI 时默认允许并须披露，但课程负责人仍可为具体任务限制或禁止用途；把大量 GenAI 内容当作本人作品提交和／或未披露仍构成违规。

records.statement: Microsoft Copilot Chat is the only AI service approved here for University data. Approved use requires UofG credentials and enterprise data protection; output must be reviewed by a human. Confidential or sensitive University or third-party information should not be put into AI tools, and AI tools are not recommended for confidential meetings. Tool access does not grant assessment permission.

scope.audience: students
qualifiers: Current 2026/27 guidance and Code 32; older published claims are a separately dated record. Assessments set under earlier rules retain their applicable instructions.

evidence.quote:
Microsoft Copilot Chat
The University-approved Generative AI platform
Microsoft Copilot Chat is a Generative AI tool that uses the same large language models as Open AI’s ChatGPT, but with added security.
It is the only AI service approved for use with University data
It is your copilot for work; it should never be trusted with unsupervised decisions. Anything Copilot produces must be reviewed by a human.
Microsoft Copilot Chat is available from:
Microsoft 365
Microsoft Teams
Microsoft Copilot app on your mobile device.
You must be logged in with your UofG credentials to use Copilot Chat or this is not an approved use and will not meet the University’s security requirements.
Always check for the green shield at the top of your chat, it indicates that enterprise data protection is in place.
At a glance
Copilot Chat is the only AI service approved for use with University data.
Anything Copilot produces must be reviewed by a human.
Always check for the green shield – it shows you are logged in and enterprise data protection is in place
AI tools are not recommended for use in confidential meetings
Get Copilot
Using other AI services
Confidential or sensitive information (including, for example, IP) belonging to the University or any third party should not be put into AI tools

records.statement: The current teaching guidance says the University does not employ AI detection tools and misconduct investigations should never rely on that software. Staff should not upload student work to detection platforms or external systems. Investigations must use all available evidence; the listed indicators do not automatically mean a student used or misused GenAI. Exploratory interviews, a response statement or earlier drafts may be requested before referral.

scope.audience: students
qualifiers: Current 2026/27 guidance and Code 32; older published claims are a separately dated record. Assessments set under earlier rules retain their applicable instructions.

evidence.quote:
Academic Judgement, Not Detection Software
The University does not employ AI detection tools, and academic misconduct investigations should never rely upon such software. Staff should not upload student work to AI detection platforms or other external systems, as this may breach data protection requirements and compromise student privacy.
Academic judgement – based on familiarity with students’ capabilities and understanding of how AI-generated content typically presents – provides a more reliable basis for identifying concerns that warrant further investigation.
Indicators That May Warrant Further Inquiry
Submitted work that raises concerns might exhibit a range of characteristics and the Senate Assessors for Student Conduct have created enhanced guidance which distinguishes between compelling evidence of GenAI misuse, as well as other indicators of potential GenAI misuse.
Content and argumentation
generic or formulaic language lacking disciplinary specificity
surface-level treatment of complex topics without sustained critical analysis
confident presentation of plausible-sounding but inaccurate information
generic conclusions that fail to address the specific question posed
lack of specific examples or detailed engagement with sources
References and citations
fabricated or non-existent references
misattributed quotations or garbled author names
inconsistencies in citation formatting
references that exist but do not support the claims made
Style and presentation
verbose or exaggeratedly formal language
repetitive phrasing or circular argumentation
unnaturally smooth transitions lacking substantive logical development
unexpected Americanisms in otherwise British English writing (and vice versa)
marked inconsistency with the student’s previous work.
Any misconduct investigation must be based on the all the available evidence and conducted in accordance with University procedures. Before referral under the Code of Student Conduct processes, staff may undertake an ‘exploratory interview’ with the student, request a statement in response to the allegations and/or request to see earlier drafts. Note that the presence of the above characteristics does not automatically mean the student has used or misused GenAI tools. [UofG Login required].

localSummary.zh: 当前教学指导明确称大学不采用 AI 检测工具，违规调查不应依赖此类软件；教职员不应把学生作品上传检测平台或外部系统。调查须依据全部可用证据，所列特征不自动证明使用或滥用 GenAI；正式移交前可以探索性访谈、要求回应陈述或早期草稿。

qualifiers: Student casework guidance; March 2023 formal policy retained separately, with postgraduate research scope exclusions.

evidence.quote:
The tabs below include the policy and procedural documentation in relation to student casework. If you are considering making a complaint or appeal, or are subject to any form of conduct proceedings, you are strongly encouraged to seek advice and support such as from your personal tutor, department or faculty senior tutor (see list here), or from the Student Union Advice Centre (see details here).
If you are unsure of the relevant procedure or form that you should be using, please contact the student casework team through student.complaints@imperial.ac.uk or student.appeals@imperial.ac.uk

records.statement: Misusing generative AI can breach the Academic Integrity Policy, including using generative AI in assessments where prohibited, submitting AI-generated work without appropriate acknowledgment, or inputting University teaching/course materials, another student's content, external intellectual property, or personal/health information into AI tools.

scope.audience: students

conditions: in an assessment where use of generative AI has been prohibited
submitting AI-generated work without appropriate acknowledgment
inputting University teaching or course materials, content generated by another student, Intellectual Property from external partners, or any person's personal or health information into AI tools

evidence.quote:
Unauthorised or inappropriate use of generative artificial intelligence
Misusing generative AI can breach the Academic Integrity Policy. Examples include:
using generative AI such as chatbots, paraphrasing tools or translation tools in an assessment where their use has been prohibited
submitting AI-generated work without appropriate acknowledgment
inputting University teaching or course materials, content generated by another student, Intellectual Property from external partners, or any person’s personal or health information into AI tools.
To find more information about the use of AI in assessable work, visit our artificial intelligence page.

localSummary.zh: 学生指导列举可能违反学术诚信规则的 AI 滥用：在禁止的评估中使用、提交而未适当注明，或向工具输入大学教学材料、他人作品、外部知识产权及个人/健康信息。需结合实际任务要求，不是使用工具就自动违规。

zh: 不是使用工具就自动违规

records.statement: Turnitin AI detection tool may be used to evaluate suspected unpermitted or unacknowledged generative AI use, but the AI detector score cannot be the only evidence relied upon for an academic integrity case and will be considered alongside other relevant evidence.

scope.audience: students

conditions: marker or teacher suspects that part or all of assessment has been generated using AI technology and its use was not permitted, or use was not acknowledged
exceptions: AI detector score would not be the only evidence relied upon for an academic integrity case

evidence.quote:
Detecting generative AI use
Turnitin has a tool for detecting use of artificial intelligence in student work. If a marker or teacher suspects that part or all of your assessment has been generated using AI technology and its use was not permitted, or use was not acknowledged, the Turnitin AI detection tool may be used to evaluate the situation.
It’s important to note that the AI detector score would not be the only evidence relied upon for an academic integrity case, but will be considered alongside other relevant evidence.

localSummary.zh: 学生指导称可用 Turnitin AI 检测辅助评估未获许可或未注明的疑虑，但检测分数不能成为案件唯一依据，须与其他相关证据一起考虑。此条与文本相似度报告不同。

zh: 不能成为案件唯一依据

records.statement: For major academic integrity breaches, the Faculty Educational Integrity team conducts an initial investigation and must provide written notice informing the student of the allegation, response instructions, response timeframe, and requesting a meeting attendance or written response before deciding if the allegation is substantiated.

scope.audience: students

conditions: matter relates to a potentially more serious academic integrity breach
before determining if the allegation has been substantiated

evidence.quote:
Outcome and investigation
If the matter relates to a potentially more serious academic integrity breach, the Faculty Educational Integrity team will carry out an initial investigation in which they will consider why the incident was reported.
Before determining if the allegation has been substantiated, the Faculty Educational Integrity team will give you written notice that:
informs you of the allegation
provides instructions on how you should respond and a timeframe to respond
requests you to attend a meeting or submit a written response.
Once you have responded to the formal allegation, or the time allowed for you to respond has elapsed, the Faculty Educational Integrity team will consider your response and the evidence. All available evidence will be considered. This may include the work you submitted, similarity-detection software reports from Turnitin, source publications, examination incident reports and prohibited materials confiscated during an examination.

localSummary.zh: 较严重疑虑由 Faculty Educational Integrity 团队先调查；认定前须书面通知指控、回应方式和回应时限，并要求开会或书面回应。此段未提供统一天数，应看自己的通知。

records.statement: When a student is requested to attend an allegation meeting, it usually takes about 15 to 20 minutes and includes at least the student, the faculty Educational Integrity Coordinator, and a faculty professional staff member, with permission to bring a support person, and occasionally the teacher or examination invigilator may also be asked to attend.

scope.audience: students

conditions: student is requested to attend a meeting

evidence.quote:
If you are requested to attend a meeting, it will usually take about 15 to 20 minutes and will include at least you, the Educational Integrity Coordinator from your faculty, and a professional staff member from the faculty. You can bring a support person, and occasionally your teacher or examination invigilator (supervisor) will also be asked to attend.
Be cautious of external companies claiming to assist with academic cases. They falsely advertise high success rates, charge high fees, and may encourage unethical practices. They also are not acquainted with the University’s systems and processes.

localSummary.zh: 指导称疑虑会议通常约 15–20 分钟，由学生、学院 Educational Integrity Coordinator 和专业职员参加；学生可带支持人，有时教师或监考人也会参加。这是通常会议时长，不是提交期限。

records.statement: The most serious instances of suspected cheating, including contract cheating or repeated breaches, are classified as misconduct, governed by the University of Sydney (Student Discipline) Rule, and handled by the Registrar.

scope.audience: students

conditions: most serious instances of suspected cheating, contract cheating, repeated academic integrity breaches, or breaches deemed to warrant a larger penalty than for major breaches

evidence.quote:
The most serious instances of suspected cheating are handled under the misconduct process, which is governed by the University of Sydney (Student Discipline) Rule and handled by the Registrar.
On this page
Levels of breaches and their outcomes
Responding to an allegation
Turnitin
Reporting suspected breaches

Misconduct
Misconduct includes contract cheating, repeated academic integrity breaches, or breaches deemed by the decision maker to warrant a larger penalty than for those available for ‘major’ breaches.
Misconduct has the same meaning as is outlined in the University of Sydney (Student Discipline) Rule, and will be dealt with in the same manner.

records.statement: The University of Sydney student information page states: Before responding to an academic integrity allegation in writing or at a meeting, students are recommended to seek free, confidential, and independent advice and guidance from the Students' Representative Council (for undergraduate students) or the Sydney University Postgraduate Representative Association (SUPRA, for postgraduate students).

scope.audience: students

conditions: before responding to an allegation either at a meeting or in writing

evidence.quote:
Responding to an allegation
Before you respond to an allegation either at a meeting or in writing, we recommend seeking advice and support from one of the independent student advocacy services. These services are free, confidential and independent of the University. Their caseworkers are well-versed in university processes and can guide you through the best course of action.
Undergraduate: contact the Caseworker Help service provided by the Students’ Representative Council
Postgraduate: contact the Postgraduate Advocacy Service provided by the Sydney University Postgraduate Representative Association (SUPRA).
If you are requested to attend a meeting, it will usually take about 15 to 20 minutes and will include at least you, the Educational Integrity Coordinator from your faculty, and a professional staff member from the faculty. You can bring a support person, and occasionally your teacher or examination invigilator (supervisor) will also be asked to attend.

records.statement: The University of Sydney student information page states: Students found to have committed a minor academic integrity breach are required to complete an approved development course and may receive a small remedial mark reduction; minor breaches may be determined locally by the unit coordinator unless the student has a prior breach on record.

scope.audience: students

conditions: it has been determined that student committed a minor academic integrity breach
student has no prior record of an academic integrity breach to be handled locally
exceptions: If you have a prior record of an academic integrity breach, the case cannot be handled locally by your unit coordinator and will instead be directed to the Faculty’s Educational Integrity team to be assessed.

evidence.quote:
Outcome and investigation
If it has been determined that you have committed a minor academic integrity breach, you will be sent a letter (via email) outlining the steps to resolve the matter.
You will be required to complete an approved development course and may receive a small, remedial mark reduction to remove any advantage that could be gained through inappropriate academic practice.
This is an opportunity for you to learn about the required standards of referencing and improve for future assessments.
Minor breaches (such as those relating to low-level plagiarism or recycling of previously assessed material) may be determined locally by your unit coordinator. If you have a prior record of an academic integrity breach, the case cannot be handled locally by your unit coordinator and will instead be directed to the Faculty’s Educational Integrity team to be assessed.

records.statement: The University of Sydney student information page states: Engaging in contract cheating can result in failing the unit of study, suspension, or expulsion from the University under the University of Sydney (Student Discipline) Rule.

scope.audience: students

conditions: engaging in contract cheating

evidence.quote:
The University takes contract cheating, misconduct and impersonation very seriously and applies severe penalties under the University of Sydney (Student Discipline) Rule.
Engaging in contract cheating can result in failing your unit of study, or even suspension or expulsion from the University. Cheating could also undermine your future employment and career prospects and may affect your registration with professional associations, employer groups, and federations.
Contract cheating is also illegal under Australian law.

records.statement: For a finding or penalty made by the Registrar, a disciplinary appeal to SDAC must be submitted within 20 working days of receiving the penalty notice. Grounds concern an unreasonable or unsupported finding, or an excessive or inappropriate penalty. To request extra time, contact the Student Affairs Unit before the deadline with reasons and supporting documents; an approved extension is confirmed in writing. This route is distinct from academic appeals.

scope.audience: students
qualifiers: Academic review/SAB and Registrar disciplinary/SDAC routes must be kept distinct; guidance last updated 2 June 2026.

evidence.quote:
How appeals work If you have been the subject of a misconduct process where a finding and/or penalty has been made by the Registrar, you may wish to appeal to the Student Disciplinary Appeals Committee (SDAC) on either of the following grounds: you consider the finding of misconduct to be unreasonable or it cannot be supported you consider the penalty to be imposed as being excessive or inappropriate. Timing your appeal To be eligible for a disciplinary appeal, you will need to submit your appeal within 20 working days of receiving your penalty notice from the Registrar. Contact Student Affairs Unit _self

If you require longer than the 20 working days to submit your appeal, you need to email the Student Affairs Unit before the deadline.

You will need to provide a reason why you should be granted an extension to submit your appeal and include documents that support the extension request.

If your extension is approved, you will be provided written advice on the new deadline for your submission.

records.statement: The academic-appeals guidance sets a faculty or Academic Panel review application within 20 working days of receiving the informal-resolution outcome, original academic decision, or most recent decision about it. A later SAB appeal is within 15 working days of receiving the faculty or Panel review outcome, unless an extension is granted. A specific problem in how that review was decided is required; disagreement alone is insufficient. Check the applicable academic-integrity route rather than using the Registrar disciplinary clock.

scope.audience: students
qualifiers: Academic review/SAB and Registrar disciplinary/SDAC routes must be kept distinct; guidance last updated 2 June 2026.

evidence.quote:
Level 2: Apply for faculty or Academic Panel review
If an informal resolution doesn’t resolve your concerns, the next level available to you is to apply for a review from the relevant faculty or administrative unit.
You must apply within 20 working days of receiving:
an outcome from your request for informal resolution
the original academic decision, or
the most recent decision made about the original decision.
It is important to include everything you want the faculty or Academic Panel to consider when you apply for this review. This includes your reasons for disagreeing with the decision and any documents or evidence that support your application.
ispopup: false How to apply for review ispopup:
Level 3: Appeal to the Student Appeals Body (SAB)
You cannot appeal to the SAB simply because you disagree with the faculty or Academic Panel review outcome.
If you believe there is a specific problem with how the faculty or Academic Panel review decision was made, then you may be able to appeal to the SAB. This is the final level of the academic appeals process.
If you apply for a SAB appeal, you must apply within 15 working days of receiving the outcome of your faculty or Academic Panel review. If you are granted an extension, you must apply within the extended timeframe.

scope.audience: students
qualifiers: 2026/27 Academic Conduct and Practice Handbook, updated August 2026; coursework and supervised examination tariffs are separate.

evidence.quote:
GenAI Use in Assessments
This is a guide to the University of Exeter's AI in assessment guidance.
If you are not sure what is expected for a particular assessment after reading your assessment brief and all of the information on this page, please speak to your module lead before you complete the assessment.
Please note: While this page may look different compared to the 2025/6 academic year, the AI in assessments guidance has remained the same for the 2026/7 academic year. We have only streamlined the content of this page for ease of understanding.
The University of Exeter follows a four-tier approach to GenAI use in assessments:
AI-integrated
The use of GenAI tools is required by the module’s Intended Learning Outcomes.
Your assessment brief will include an explanation of how AI should (and should not) be used and a checklist of purposes for AI use.
You must include GenAI prompts and, where possible, hyperlinks to their output as part of your submission. You may like to use the 'record of GenAI use' template provided on the 'Recording and Referencing GenAI' guide. If hyperlinks are not produced through the tools you use, save the AI-generated output in a document that you can easily access later (e.g. on OneDrive). You may be asked to produce this material in the event of an academic conduct inquiry.
You must never use AI to translate more than a word or short phrase into English unless agreed in the checked boxes in your assessment brief.
AI-assisted
You can choose to use GenAI tools ethically and responsibly to assist in the development of an assessment.
The assessment brief will include a checklist of purposes that AI can be used for.
If you choose to use GenAI tools in AI-assisted assessments, you must include GenAI prompts and, where possible, hyperlinks to their output as part of your submission. You may like to use the 'record of GenAI use' template provided on the 'Recording and Referencing GenAI' guide. If hyperlinks are not produced through the tools you use, save the AI-generated output in a document that you can easily access later (e.g. on OneDrive). You may be asked to produce this material in the event of an academic conduct inquiry.
You must never use AI to translate more than a word or short phrase into English unless agreed in the checked boxes in your assessment brief.
AI-minimal
You may use AI tools for checking spelling and grammar mistakes only, with no other impact on the structure or content of the assessment. This includes AI tools such as Microsoft Word's grammar and spelling checker, and not GenAI tools such as Microsoft Copilot or ChatGPT. This is because using AI tools outside of these uses prevents fair assessment of your ability to achieve module learning outcomes.
While completing AI-minimal assessments, you may find that some search tools you are using have GenAI features, such as source summarisation tools. Do not copy, paste or paraphrase information from these AI-generated summaries.
AI-prohibited
You must not use GenAI tools under any circumstances when preparing and writing for this assessment. This is because using GenAI tools prevents fair assessment of your ability to demonstrate module learning outcomes.
Submitting your assessment
No matter what category of AI use your assessment is, when you finish your work, ask yourself: 'Who is the author of this work?'. Make sure you can confidently answer 'me' before you submit your assessment.
When you submit your assessment to ELE, you will need to check a box to confirm that you have complied with the University's policy on academic conduct, and with the expectations regarding the use of GenAI as specified in your assessment brief.  It will not be possible to submit your assessment without checking this box.
Further information

evidence.quote:
If you are using a GenAI tool as part of your academic work, please check that you have followed this guidance:
A. If you are not sure whether and how you can use GenAI in your academic work, please check your assignment brief and discuss with your module lead.
B. You must never upload sensitive or identifying material to an AI tool.
C. You must never present material that has been generated by AI as your own work or the work of someone else.
D. GenAI tools should not be used to generate content which is included in an assessment without following guidance on acknowledging and referencing GenAI. This would be an offence under the University’s Academic Conduct and Practice policy.
E. It is important to note that GenAI tools do not always output accurate or unbiased information. You must therefore critically analyse and verify any information that you plan to use in your academic work, including any references or sources provided by a GenAI tool.

records.statement: The 2026/27 Handbook defines academic offences by unfair advantage or deception. Plagiarism includes representing work or ideas as your own without appropriate acknowledgement, including copying from AI-generated content. The examples are illustrative, not exhaustive.

scope.audience: students
qualifiers: 2026/27 Academic Conduct and Practice Handbook, updated August 2026; coursework and supervised examination tariffs are separate.

evidence.quote:
1.  Offences and Definitions 
1.1 An academic offence is defined as an act or failure to act that if undetected gives, or  
aims to give, an advantage over other students, or any behaviour which may deceive  
those setting, administering and marking a piece of work. Academic offences can take 
number of forms (please note that the examples listed alongside each offence are 
intended to be illustrative and are not exhaustive): 
 
a.  Plagiarism, i.e. the act of representing work or ideas as one’s own without 
appropriate acknowledgement or referencing. For instance: 
i.  Direct copying of text, or illustrations, from a book, article, fellow student's essay, 
handout, thesis, web page, AI -generated content, or other source (including a 
source originally in another language) without proper acknowledgement. 
ii.  Claiming individual ideas derived from a book, article etc. as one's own, and

evidence.quote:
5. Arrangements for Department and Faculty level meetings 
5.1 The Meeting Request Letter  should be sent at least five working days  prior to the 
meeting.  
5.2 All relevant documentation should be made available to the student five working days 
prior to the meeting. 
5.3 If the Faculty (or delegated School) appointed an Investigating Officer, then their report 
should be made available to the Student as part of the relevant documentation sent to 
the student five working days in advance of the meeting. The Panel may call the

Investigating Officer to present their findings but must notify the Student of their

5.4 A witness is a person who can testify their knowledge of a matter that is under

evidence.quote:
9. ACADEMIC MISCONDUCT COMMITTEE PRODEDURE 
9.1 The procedure for an investigation conducted by the Academic Misconduct 
Committee will follow the arrangements contained in this section. 
9.2 Before a meeting of the Academic Misconduct Committee is arranged, the 
student will be asked if they wish to have an in-person meeting on Keele Campus 
with the Committee or if they wish the meeting to take place on MS Teams. Once 
the student has confirmed this, a meeting of the Academic Misconduct 
Committee will be arranged. 
9.3 The student will be emailed a letter inviting them to the meeting of the Academic 
Misconduct Committee. The letter will also set out the nature of the allegation and a copy 
of the documentation that will be presented to the Committee. This letter will be sent to 
the student normally a minimum of 7 calendar days in advance of the meeting. 
9.4 The Committee will be made aware of all previous offences of academic misconduct when 
considering a case. Unproven offences will not be disclosed to the Committee (see section 
15.6). The student will be given a copy of the relevant documents that the Committee is 
given that relate to these previous offences. 
9.5 The student will be informed of their right to call witnesses, give evidence and to be 
accompanied (see section 8 for who is allowed to accompany a student). 
9.6 The student will be informed that, if they are not able to attend the meeting on the 
arranged day, they must inform the Student Appeals, Complaints and Conduct Team in 
writing giving the reason why. The team will consult with the Chair of the Academic 
Misconduct Committee to decide if there is good reason for the meeting to be postponed to 
a later date. 
9.7 The student can submit a response to the allegation. This must be received at least 48 hours 
prior to the meeting and must include any previously unknown circumstances and 
supporting evidence which could support them. The Committee can ignore any 
circumstances discussed at the meeting that were either not included in the student 
response or not accompanied by supporting evidence. This statement will be given to the 
presenting member of staff (see section 19.17) and the Committee.

records.statement: The general tariff applies across academic levels. Conduct Officers assess plagiarism or collusion severity and previous offences. For proven cases the Committee may choose an appropriate proportionate penalty beyond the tariff; termination requires Academic Registrar ratification, and on appeal any termination requires Vice-Chancellor ratification. These are conditional powers, not automatic AI sanctions.

scope.audience: students
qualifiers: Student Academic Misconduct Code of Practice v2.5, commenced 1 September 2025; different Officer and Committee appeal routes.

evidence.quote:
12. PENALTIES ISSUED BY ACADEMIC CONDUCT OFFICERS 
12.1 The tariff sets out the scope of the Academic Conduct Officer’s jurisdiction and the fixed 
levels of penalty available to them. It applies to students in programmes at all academic 
levels. 
12.2 The Academic Conduct Officers will use their academic judgement in plagiarism and 
collusion cases to decide if a case is poor academic practice, a minor, or a major offence. 
They will take into account the level of study, background of study, nature of the 
assessment, the quality of the copied text, and any previous offences on record. 
12.3 The Academic Conduct Officer can require a student to take additional instruction in the 
expectations and requirements of academic study and behaviour. For first offences of 
plagiarism, Academic Conduct Officers should ensure that students have the opportunity to 
learn from their mistake and direct them to appropriate support and guidance. 
 
13. PENALTIES ISSUED BY ACADEMIC MISCONDUCT COMMITTEE 
13.1 In proven cases, the Committee can impose any of the penalties set out in the tariff but is 
not restricted to these and can impose another penalty provided this is appropriate and 
proportionate. If the Academic Misconduct Committee decides that a student’s studies 
should be terminated, the decision must be ratified by the  Academic Registrar. If the 
student appeals, the appeal will be heard by the Academic Misconduct Appeals Committee 
(see section 16) and any decision for termination of studies must be ratified by the Vice-
Chancellor. 
PAGE 13
Page 13 of 25 
 
13.2 Where an educational  partner holds its own Academic Misconduct Committee, any 
penalties must be approved by the Head of Student Appeals, Complaints and Conduct 
before they are imposed. This is to ensure consistency with similar cases dealt with by 
Keele’s Academic Misconduct Committee. 
13.3 The tariff below lists the penalties that will normally be applied for a proven offence. The 
Committee will consider the standard penalty in relation to the type of offence and will 
decide if it is appropriate taking into account the following: 
a) The academic level of the student; 
b) Extent of the plagiarism or collusion (minor/major); 
c) Previous academic misconduct history of the student; 
d) Exceptional circumstances (see section 11.4); 
e) Any procedural irregularities; 
f) Evidence of any intention to deceive; 
g) Nature of the work.

records.statement: A Conduct Officer decision can be appealed to the Academic Misconduct Committee on procedural irregularity or substantiated exceptional circumstances with valid reasons for not raising them earlier. A Committee decision can be appealed to a differently constituted Appeals Committee on procedural irregularity or previously unknown substantiated new evidence with valid reasons for earlier omission, except where the Committee itself heard an appeal against an Officer. The Code says appeals must be sent to the Head of Student Appeals, Complaints and Conduct within ten calendar days of the date on the outcome letter.

evidence.quote:
16. APPEALS 
16.1 A student has the right to appeal to the Academic Misconduct Committee against the 
decision of an Academic Conduct Officer. Appeals can be made only on one or both of the 
following grounds: 
I. procedural irregularity in the conduct of the original investigations of the 
Academic Conduct Officer; 
II. exceptional circumstances, providing that these circumstances can be 
substantiated and there is a valid reason why these were not made known at the 
time when the penalty was imposed. 
 
16.2 A student can appeal the decision of the Academic Misconduct Committee (to the 
Academic Misconduct Appeals Committee), unless the Academic Misconduct 
Committee’s decision was on an appeal against the decision of an Academic Conduct 
Officer. The membership of the Academic Misconduct Appeals Committee must be 
different to the original committee membership when the appeal is heard. Appeals can 
only be made on one or both of the following grounds: 
I. procedural irregularity prior to or in the conduct of the Committee meeting; 
II. there is new evidence that can be substantiated, including exceptional 
circumstances, which were not known at the time and may have affected the 
outcome had it been known to the Committee and that there is a valid reason for 
not making it known at the time. 
16.3 Appeals must be sent to the Head of Student Appeals, Complaints and Conduct within 10 
calendar days of the date on the letter informing the student of the outcome. 
16.4 Appeals will be considered in the first instance by two members of the Academic 
Misconduct Committee. This is called the sifting stage of the appeals process. It consists 
of an initial assessment of readily available documentation, to include the student 
PAGE 20
Page 20 of 25 
 
submission, information on SCIMS, and the paperwork from the case considered by 
either the Academic Conduct Officer or the Academic Misconduct Committee. 
16.5 If it is clear that a case for consideration has not been established including a valid reason 
as to why the student did not use the exceptional circumstances process if they ask for 
exceptional circumstances to be taken into account, the case may be rejected.

evidence.quote:
Student academic misconduct appeals against decisions made by Academic Misconduct Committee
Student Academic Misconduct Appeals against decisions made by Academic Misconduct Committee
Student academic misconduct appeals are initiated by the student in accordance with Regulation D4, and the accompanying Student Academic Misconduct Code of Practice The purpose of the academic misconduct appeals process is to allow all students to appeal against decisions of the Academic Misconduct Committee, unless it was an appeal against the decision of an Academic Conduct Officer.
Appeals may only be made on one or both of the following grounds:
a) Any procedural irregularity prior to or in the conduct of the Committee meeting;
b) there is new evidence that can be substantiated, including exceptional circumstances, which was not known at the time, and may have affected the outcome had it been known to the Committee and that there is a valid reason for not making it known at the time.
You must submit your appeal in writing to the Student Appeals, Complaints and Conduct Manager within 10 calendar days (not including University closed days or Bank Holidays, but including weekends) from the date of the letter sent to you informing you of the decision of the Academic Misconduct Committee. With your appeal should be sent any supporting evidence.
Appeals will be considered first by two members of the Academic Misconduct Committee not previously involved in the case. This is called the 'sifting' stage of the process. It consists of an initial assessment of readily available documentation, including your submission, information on the Student Record System and the paperwork considered by the Academic Misconduct Committee. If it is clear that that there is no case (i.e. you have not fulfilled one or both of the grounds case for the appeal to be considered), the appeal will be rejected and you will be informed of the decision in writing, stating the reasons why. If there is a case for appeal, a meeting of the Academic Misconduct Appeals Committee will be convened and you will be invited to attend.
You will be given no less than 7 calendar days’ notice of the date, time and location of the hearing.
The membership of the Academic Misconduct Appeals Committee will be different to the original Committee membership when the appeal is heard.

8.2 The role of the supporter is to attend the meeting with the student as moral support and to 
assist them in presenting their case to the Academic Conduct Officer or the Academic 
Committee, and to seek clarification on any procedural matters.  The supporter may confer 
with the student during the meeting.  It is expected that the student will answer any 
questions from the Committee themselves, though the student may confer with the 
supporter before answering.    The supporter may read a pre-prepared statement on behalf 
of the student, with the student’s consent, and the permission of the Chair. 
 
8.3 We recognise that the process may be an upsetting and stressful process for all parties, and 
whilst students at the University are expected to have demonstrated a reasonable level of 
English-language proficiency on entry, we also recognise that a stressful process might 
require additional support if a student’s first language in not English. The University will not 
object to a Supporter providing a reasonable amount of translation support at meetings, 
but the University will mitigate the requirement for this wherever possible to ensure the

evidence.quote: iii. If the Course Director or AIA considers the student has engaged in poor academic practice, they must notify the student of the finding and provide them with the details of the incident and the proposed outcome. The student will be informed of the time available to submit a written response (five working days) and that the process will proceed without a response where that time is exceeded.

vii. Where the Academic Head confirms the finding of poor academic practice, or where the student does not respond within five working days to the initial notification, the student will be advised in writing of the finding of poor academic practice and the outcome (including adjustment of marks where appropriate).

viii. The advice to the student must also include a recommendation for the student to take up further educative options. evidence.quote:
### b. Suspected academic misconduct in tests or coursework (including research components of less than 30 points)

A staff member, student, or any other person may report a suspected incident of academic misconduct in coursework or a test.

The following procedures must be followed for suspected academic misconduct in coursework or tests:

i. Details of alleged incidents will be received and reviewed by the Course Director or AIA.

ii. Where the Course Director or AIA considers the student may have engaged in academic misconduct, or the Academic Head refers a poor academic practice case back to be investigated by the Course Director or AIA as potential academic misconduct, the student must be advised:

- of their opportunity to respond to the allegation and to detail any extenuating circumstances in their case; and

iii. The Course Director or AIA may invite the student to attend an interview to discuss the allegation. Where an interview is conducted, the Course Director or AIA must conduct the interview with another staff member present (unless the interview is conducted online and recorded). records.statement: The TeachWell Lane 2 guide says AI use by itself is not misconduct: decisions focus on conduct, instructions and output integrity. It distinguishes quality/rubric issues, poor academic practice and minor/major misconduct, and notes a breach may exist without intent.

scope.audience: teachers and programme teams
qualifiers: Lane 2 only; guidance does not establish every course’s 2026 adoption

evidence.quote:
The use of AI does not in and of itself constitute academic misconduct. In Lane 2 assessment, AI use is unrestricted. However, students remain fully responsible for the accuracy, and integrity, of all submitted work. Academic integrity decisions must therefore focus on student behaviour and outputs, not that they have used AI. Judgements should centre on:
Honesty and accountability (student responsibility for submitted work)
Compliance with assessment instructions
Integrity of scholarly practice (e.g., accurate attribution, valid evidence)
In short, a student could use AI to breach academic integrity, but use of AI in and of itself is not a breach; it depends on how it is used and what the assessment instructions are.

Important clarification on intent and breach
A breach can occur without intent.
Intent determines severity, not whether a breach exists.
Students remain responsible for outputs even where AI has contributed errors.

localSummary.zh: TeachWell 的 Lane 2 指导指出：仅使用 AI 本身不构成学术不端，判断关注行为、任务要求及提交内容的诚信；无意也可能构成违规，意图影响严重程度。不能把此指导套到 Lane 1 或其他不同规则。

scope.unit: University Turnitin account as described by TeachWell
scope.audience: teaching staff

evidence.quote:
What about Turnitin's AI detection feature?
With the rise of Generative AI, Turnitin introduced an AI detection tool, which adds to the similarity report in Feedback Studio. The University of Auckland piloted this tool and requested that Turnitin does not enable this feature for our account when it was released on 5 April 2023. A growing number of Australian and UK institutions have taken the same action following concerns around its lack of testing and transparency as to how it works and its effectiveness.
Are submitted assessments used by Turnitin for AI training purposes?
No. Because our University has not activated the Turnitin AI detection feature. Students' submitted assessments are not used to train Turnitin's AI models.

records.statement: The student guide describes Lane 1 as AI-restricted by default with explicitly stated course exceptions, and Lane 2 as uncontrolled assessment where AI assistance is not restricted. It says all courses will identify lanes from 2027; many begin in 2026, so students should ask their Course Director/Coordinator.

scope.audience: students
qualifiers: Two-lane rollout: all courses from 2027; not all 2026 assessments

evidence.quote:
Artificial Intelligence in assessment
The university takes the position that AI has no agency. What this means is that the student who is prompting the AI tool is to be treated as the author. As the author, each student is responsible for the work generated by the AI tool, and this may include expressly acknowledging the use of the tool. Students must be aware of the limitations of AI and treat the output critically. Ultimately, students are responsible for the work that is submitted for assessment.
Two-lane approach to assessment
The University is adopting a two-lane approach to assessment to provide clarity to students on when and how they may use AI tools in taught courses. The two lanes work in tandem to ensure that assessments:
Authentically assess students’ core knowledge and skills.
Encourage the critical and responsible use of AI.
Adapt to evolving AI capabilities and are inclusive, transparent and accessible.
The two-lane approach differentiates between controlled assessments where AI use is restricted, and other assessments where AI may be used.
Lane 1: Controlled assessment
Lane 2: Uncontrolled assessment
Definition
Graded assessment undertaken in controlled conditions and AI is restricted, by default.
Certain AI tools may be permitted in some courses but only where explicitly stated.
Graded or ungraded assessment undertaken in uncontrolled conditions.
Students may use AI to assist them, and this use is not restricted.

Students are not permitted to use AI tools in Lane 1 assessments.
Students are responsible for the work they submit for assessment, but are not restricted on the use of AI.
Courses using the two-lane approach
From 2027, all courses will explicitly identify which assessments are ‘Lane 1’ and which are ‘Lane 2’. Many courses will start to use these terms in 2026. Students should refer to their Course Director/Course Coordinator for guidance.

evidence.quote:

Advice for students on using Generative AI in coursework

records.statement: For Lane 2, TeachWell says using AI is not in itself academic misconduct, while other integrity breaches still matter. Auckland does not endorse third-party AI detectors because of unreliability, false positives and potential student-data training. This does not prove that no individual uses an external detector.

scope.audience: teaching staff and students checking Lane 2 scope
qualifiers: Two-lane rollout: all courses from 2027, many in 2026; Law School assessed-work rules retain separate faculty scope. Current Student Academic Conduct Statute page reviewed 15 October 2025.

evidence.quote:
Does academic integrity still apply to a Lane 2 assessment?
With respect to academic integrity and AI use, part of the appeal of Two-Lane Approach is that it has the potential to shift our focus away from policing student misuse of AI, to enabling students to be ethical, discerning and productive users of these tools. It also responds to student concern more widely around being falsely accused of inappropriate AI use. This is not to say that there may be other aspects of academic integrity behaviour and breaches that are still relevant, only that the act of using AI is, in and of itself, not academic misconduct.
In thinking about AI, we take the position that it has no agency, so the user (student) who is prompting these tools is to be treated as the author. They are responsible for the work generated by the ‘model’; this may include express acknowledgement. It is important that students are aware of the limitations of AI and treat the output critically since they are responsible for that output.
What about students who cheat? Can AI detection software help?
The Two-Lane Approach is built on the principle that using AI appropriately is not cheating. Detection tools will always lag behind the latest AI models. They are also more likely to catch students who use AI poorly or who lack access to premium tools - raising valid equity concerns.
Instead of relying on detection, teachers are encouraged to focus on:
Assessment design that integrates AI use transparently
Stating clear expectations for students
Strategic use of Lane 1 assessments which support students to achieve learning outcomes
The University of Auckland does not endorse the use of third-party AI detection tools, as these may be unreliable, create false positives, and may use student data to train their models.

localSummary.zh: 针对 Lane 2，TeachWell 说明使用 AI 本身不构成学术违规，但其他诚信违规仍须考虑。Auckland 不认可第三方 AI 检测工具，理由包括不可靠、误报和学生数据可能用于训练；这不证明任何个人都不会使用外部检测工具。

evidence.quote:
Welcome to the Library’s guide to using Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen AI) to support your literature searching. This resource aims to help you understand the benefits and limitations of using generative AI for finding literature to reference in your academic work.
Before you use any AI tool to support your assessed work, please check the guidance from your module or course and read the University’s guidance for students on using artificial intelligence in your learning.
Generative AI tools such as Microsoft Copilot can be helpful when you need to identify a topic to research and/or define a research question.
Perhaps you have an area of interest you’d like to research but need to refine into a research question or statement. Or maybe you want to get to know a little more about a topic, to give you ideas for themes or topics to research more deeply in the published literature.
You can generate prompts which will direct the Gen AI tool to help you with these tasks.

records.statement: Flinders students can access Microsoft Copilot Chat with enterprise data protection using Flinders credentials, selecting Work and checking the shield. Each topic or assessment sets permitted uses, documentation and acknowledgement. Using Copilot when it is not approved can breach academic integrity.

scope.audience: students
qualifiers: Student Academic Integrity Policy effective 10 October 2024; coursework Level 1, Statute 6.4 Level 2 and HDR research-integrity routes must remain distinct.

evidence.quote:
Flinders University students have access to Copilot Chat with enterprise data protection - this means that your chats are private, secure, and anonymous and they are not used to train the underlying AI model. Simply login with your Flinders details, following the steps below.

Steps for using Copilot Chat

Need help?
Access Copilot Chat
Go to https://m365.cloud.microsoft/ or open the Microsoft 365 App.
Microsoft Edge or Google Chrome are recommended. These allow you to engage with content on a webpage using Copilot in a side panel.
If you use a free personal Microsoft account, log out of this and follow the next steps to login through the University.
Select to ‘Sign in’.
Login with your Flinders University details (email, FAN, password).
If you are given a choice between ‘Work’ or ‘Personal’, select ‘Work’.
Check for the shield icon. This indicates that your data is protected.
Learn more about Copilot Chat data protection & security
Need help accessing Copilot Chat?

Follow these steps to make the most of Copilot Chat
1. Check that use of GenAI is approved for your topic
keyboard_arrow_up
Before using Copilot Chat, you first need to confirm if you can use GenAI tools and what you can use them for.
Each topic – and sometimes each assessment piece – will have its own guidelines for how AI tools are and are not allowed to be used. These guidelines may also indicate what information you need to provide, such as the prompts you entered and a copy of the output generated.
Check your assignment instructions or ask your teacher if you are unsure or want further clarification. The Unsure about AI? Just ask video includes some questions you can ask, or you can get some ideas from this AI Assessment Scale.
Remember, using Copilot Chat when it is not approved can be a breach of academic integrity.
Follow the instructions from your teachers on if you can use Copilot Chat, what you can use it for, what documentation you need to provide, and how to acknowledge your use.

records.statement: The Student Academic Integrity Policy includes under plagiarism an assessment portion generated by an algorithm, computer generator or AI without appropriate permission and/or acknowledgement. The policy’s categories and consequences depend on the case; AI use is not an automatic Level 2 finding.

scope.audience: students
qualifiers: Student Academic Integrity Policy effective 10 October 2024; coursework Level 1, Statute 6.4 Level 2 and HDR research-integrity routes must remain distinct.

evidence.quote:
a. Plagiarism 
When the work of another is represented, intentionally or unintentionally, as one's own original work, 
without appropriate acknowledgement of the author, creator or the source. This includes but is not limited 
to the following: 
i. paraphrasing from a source text, whether in manuscript, printed or electronic form (e.g., article 
spinning, text rewriting and content creation tools), without appropriate acknowledgement  
ii. word-for-word copying, cutting or pasting statements from a single source or multiple sources or 
piecing together work of others and representing them as original work. In cases where direct 
extracts are presented without quotation marks, it is not sufficient to merely acknowledge the 
source. 
iii. submitting as one's own work all or part of another student's work, even with the student's 
knowledge or consent 
iv. submitting an assessment task where a portion of the assessment task has been generated by an 
algorithm, computer generator or other artificial intelligence without appropriate permission and/or 
acknowledgement

localSummary.zh: Student Academic Integrity Policy 在抄袭示例中包括：评估部分内容由算法、计算机生成器或 AI 生成，却缺少适当许可和／或披露。具体类别及后果须依个案判断；使用 AI 不会自动成为 Level 2。

records.statement: In a Level 1 inquiry, the Second Reviewer gives at least five University business days’ notice, supplies the allegation and related documents, and invites a written response, attendance, or both. A permitted support person may attend. Exceptional/unforeseen circumstances can justify an extension at the reviewer’s discretion; the inquiry may proceed without the student.

scope.audience: students
qualifiers: Student Academic Integrity Policy effective 10 October 2024; coursework Level 1, Statute 6.4 Level 2 and HDR research-integrity routes must remain distinct.

evidence.quote:
b. The Level 1 Inquiry’s purpose is to determine: 
i. if the alleged failure to meet academic integrity requirements has been substantiated  
ii. the category of the failure, and 
iii. the appropriate responses in accordance with s. 5.3 of the Student Academic Integrity Policy. 
c. The Second Reviewer will set the date and time of the Level 1 Inquiry.  
d. The Second Reviewer will give the student a minimum of 5 University business days’ notice of the 
Level 1 Inquiry. 
e. The Second Reviewer will notify the student of the allegation and inquiry by email (to their University 
email address) (template available), which must include: 
i. a link to the Student Academic Integrity Policy
 and these procedures 
ii. the details of the allegation, including copies of all related documents  
iii. the time, date and place of the inquiry—the inquiry may be held in person, or using any technology 
which enables all those participating to communicate concurrently with each other and to 
participate effectively 
iv. an invitation for the student to respond to the allegation in writing, or by attendance at the inquiry 
(either in person or via technology), or both 
v. an invitation for the student to be accompanied at the meeting (either in person or via technology) 
by a support person, namely a Flinders University staff member or student or a representative of 
the Flinders University Student Association Student Assist team 
[Legal representation is not permitted, but a legally qualified student or representative may attend as a support 
person provided they are not acting in a professional legal capacity.] 
f. A student may request an extension of time to respond to the allegations due to unforeseen or 
exceptional circumstances beyond the control of the student, which may be granted at the Second 
Reviewer’s discretion. 
g. The Second Reviewer will conduct the Inquiry at the scheduled time, whether the student has 
responded to the notification or not, or is present or not. 
h. If the student is present at the Inquiry, the Second Reviewer must ensure they are given an opportunity 
to present a response. The student and their support person may be asked to leave before the final 
determination is made. 
i. Based on all the evidence before the Inquiry, the Second Reviewer will make a determination on 
whether the allegation of failure to meet academic integrity requirements has been substantiated.

records.statement: For Level 1 coursework cases, exam/test/quiz penalties differ from other assessments. A first case in other assessment may require resubmission capped at Pass or a deduction up to 100% with no resubmission/supplementary assessment. These are conditional policy options after a finding, not automatic AI sanctions.

scope.audience: students
qualifiers: Student Academic Integrity Policy effective 10 October 2024; coursework Level 1, Statute 6.4 Level 2 and HDR research-integrity routes must remain distinct.

evidence.quote:
Penalties for Level 1 Academic Misconduct 
Coursework topic: 
a. Where the failure occurs in academic 
work submitted for an examination, 
test or quiz for a topic: 
i. A deduction of up to 100% for the examination, test or quiz, 
or the relevant component 
OR 
ii. A Fail Grade for the topic, with no further option for 
assessment i.e. supplementary assessment. 
b. Where the failure occurs in academic 
work submitted for any form of 
assessment not covered by a. above—  
 
First Level 1 case: i. A requirement that the student re-submit the assessment 
task, with a maximum obtainable grade of Pass 
OR 
ii. A deduction of up to 100% of the available mark for the 
assessment task, with no option for resubmission or 
supplementary assessment.  
Second Level 1 case: 
 
i. One of the penalties available for a First Level 1 case 
OR 
ii. A Fail Grade for the topic, with a recommendation to the 
Dean (Education) that the student be permitted a 
supplementary assessment 
OR  
iii. A Fail Grade for the topic, with no further option for 
assessment i.e. supplementary assessment.

localSummary.zh: Level 1 coursework 中，考试／测验与其他评估的处分不同。其他评估的首次案件可能要求重交且最高 Pass，或扣除最高 100% 分数并不允许重交／补充评估。这是认定后的条件性政策选项，不是 AI 自动处分。

records.statement: Level 2 covers a student with two previous Level 1 records or a failure sufficiently serious to prejudice others, assessment integrity or University reputation. It is referred under Statute 6.4; possible penalties include suspension, exclusion or expulsion, rather than a mandatory result for every AI concern.

scope.audience: students
qualifiers: Student Academic Integrity Policy effective 10 October 2024; coursework Level 1, Statute 6.4 Level 2 and HDR research-integrity routes must remain distinct.

evidence.quote:
Level 2 Serious Academic Misconduct 
a. Level 2 Serious Academic Misconduct is any failure to meet academic integrity requirements by a 
student:  
i. if the student already has two records of Level 1 Academic Misconduct 
OR 
ii. if the failure is so serious that it prejudices the interest of other students, the integrity of the 
assessment scheme itself, or the reputation of the University. 
b. All allegations of Level 2 Serious Academic Misconduct will be referred for action under Statute 6.4–
Student Conduct. 
c. Any of the penalties available for Academic Misconduct Level 1 under this policy may be imposed, as 
well as any of the penalties under Statute 6.4–Student Conduct, which include suspension, exclusion 
or expulsion from the University. 
d. Where a determination of Level 2 Academic Misconduct is made, the student’s action is recorded as 
Serious Academic Misconduct on the Academic Integrity Register.

localSummary.zh: Level 2 涵盖已有两条 Level 1 记录的学生，或严重损害他人、评估诚信或学校声誉的行为，转按 Statute 6.4 处理；可能处分包括暂停、限制或开除，并非每项 AI 疑虑的必然结果。

records.statement: A Level 1 determination can be reviewed under Student Review and Appeal rules, with a further Student Appeals Committee appeal on specified grounds. Level 2 Board of Inquiry decisions instead follow the Statute 6.4 appeal procedure; do not apply the Level 1 clock to them by assumption.

7. Reviews and appeals 
a. A student may request a review of a determination of Level 1 Academic Misconduct by a Second

records.statement: A written review request under Student Review and Appeal Procedures is due within 20 University business days of being advised of the decision, unless the University accepts exceptional or compelling circumstances. Help is allowed, but the request must use the student’s own words and name with relevant decision details and evidence.

scope.audience: students
qualifiers: Student Academic Integrity Policy effective 10 October 2024; coursework Level 1, Statute 6.4 Level 2 and HDR research-integrity routes must remain distinct.

evidence.quote:
3.1. Reviews 
a. Students must request a review in writing within 20 University business days of being advised of the 
decision in their matter, unless the University considers that there are exceptional or compelling 
circumstances. 
b. Students must request a review via the University’s lodgement process
. 
c. Students may obtain assistance in preparing a request for a review from Student Advocacy and 
Welfare or from any other third party of their choosing (e.g. advocacy groups, legal representatives, 
friends or family members). However, the request must be written in a student’s own words and lodged 
under their own name. 
d. When lodging a request for review, a student should provide as much detail as possible, including:  
i. the nature and details of the original decision and any facts or documentation regarding it  
ii. the written decision of the decision-maker 
iii. their reasons for requesting the review, which may include a statement explaining why they 
consider the decision to be in error, or why they believe the consequences resulting from the 
decision are unreasonable in their circumstances.  
iv. any relevant supporting documents.

records.statement: HDR students must declare whether and how GenAI was used in research and thesis writing, discuss use and acknowledgement with supervisors, and record it at milestones. A research-integrity breach follows Breach of Research Integrity Procedures; coursework penalties are not substituted for this HDR route.

scope.audience: HDR students and supervisors
qualifiers: Student Academic Integrity Policy effective 10 October 2024; coursework Level 1, Statute 6.4 Level 2 and HDR research-integrity routes must remain distinct.

evidence.quote:
Why do I need to acknowledge the use of GenAI in my thesis?
keyboard_arrow_up
To uphold the integrity of your research and investment of your time, it is important that your research is recognised as your own and to remove any doubt for the readers. For further information please refer to a 2024 BLOG entitled Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Research.
What are the penalties for students who do not declare they have used GenAI in their thesis?
keyboard_arrow_up
It is a requirement via the HDR Policy and supporting procedures that students declare whether and how they have used GenAI in their research and thesis writing. HDR students must also abide by the Research Integrity Policy. If there is a research integrity breach, the Breach of Research Integrity Procedures will be enacted.
Can I use GenAI in my thesis?
keyboard_arrow_up
You can use GenAI in your thesis. In line with the Charter for HDR Student and Supervisor Responsibilities it is important for you to understand and discuss the University’s statement on AI in research with your supervisor(s), to understand what GenAI is, and how it can be used in research for your specific discipline. The use of GenAI must be responsible, ethical, and consistent with the core principles of research integrity that appear in the Australian Code for the Responsible Conduct of Research.
It is important to have an agreement, and open, transparent and ongoing discussions about the use of GenAI and how to declare or acknowledge it with your supervisor(s). You will be asked at each Milestone to record details of your GenAI use and discussions.
How do I acknowledge the use of GenAI in my thesis?
keyboard_arrow_up
It is important to acknowledge the use of GenAI in your thesis submitted to external examiners to allay any concerns. When you use GenAI in your research or thesis, clearly acknowledge the use of the tools in the relevant chapter. If you have not used GenAI in your research or thesis, to remove any doubt, clearly state that no GenAI has been utilised in the thesis. This can be achieved through a sentence in the introduction.
If you have used GenAI, you can easily acknowledge this with footnotes, for example: "Microsoft Copilot Chat was used to assist in the [for example: editing process and to identify improvements in writing style], in accordance with the current guidance at Flinders University."
You will be required to make a declaration about your use of GenAI in your final thesis for examination in accordance with the HDR Thesis Rules declaration.

localSummary.zh: HDR 学生须声明研究／论文是否及如何使用 GenAI，与导师讨论用途和披露，并在 Milestone 记录。研究诚信违规按 Breach of Research Integrity Procedures 处理，不能以 coursework 处分表替代此 HDR 路线。

records.statement: Flinders’ HDR guidance requires all HDR students to submit an iThenticate report with milestone written work and examination theses. It describes AI-writing detection capabilities as helping identify potential generated content and recommends ongoing supervisor conversations. This is HDR guidance, not a detector-only proof rule or a rule for all coursework students.

scope.audience: HDR students and supervisors
qualifiers: Student Academic Integrity Policy effective 10 October 2024; coursework Level 1, Statute 6.4 Level 2 and HDR research-integrity routes must remain distinct.

evidence.quote:
Can I / should I use an AI detector? What about the AI features of software (e.g., for systematic reviews) - not in 'writing' per se?
keyboard_arrow_up
At Flinders University all HDR students must submit an iThenticate report with their written work for Milestones and thesis for examination. iThenticate is a plagiarism-detection software from Turnitin, and includes AI writing detection capabilities in helping identify potential AI-generated content in submitted work.
HDR supervisors should have regular and ongoing open conversations with their students throughout candidature about the appropriate use and acknowledgement of GenAI.

records.statement: Aberdeen’s student GenAI guidance says not to outsource critical thinking, analysis, evaluation or synthesis. Generating assessed content without authorisation or acknowledgement is investigated as plagiarism under the academic discipline code.

scope.audience: students
qualifiers: Code of Practice on Student Discipline (Academic) 2026/27, approved June 2026; currently registered UG/PGT/PGR, UG/PGT graduates and visiting PGR, excluding PGR graduates. More stringent professional-body regulations take precedence.

evidence.quote:
Important: You must not use GenAI to do your critical thinking, analysis, evaluation, or 
synthesis. Neither should you use it to generate essays, poems, or any creative works. 
The purpose of these assignments is to demonstrate your unique ideas and creativity.  
Remember, using GenAI tools to generate content for work submitted for assessment, without 
authorisation or acknowledgement, will be regarded as academic misconduct and investigated as a 
plagiarism offence under the Code of Practice on Student Discipline (Academic).  You can find out 
more by watching our introductory video.

records.statement: The 2026/27 Code defines misuse of AI as unauthorised or unacknowledged generated assessment content, unless explicit permission/guidance is given as part of the assessment method. Unedited or unacknowledged generation, or failure to follow guidelines fully, may constitute misconduct; preserve the stated permission exception and may wording.

scope.audience: students
qualifiers: Code of Practice on Student Discipline (Academic) 2026/27, approved June 2026; currently registered UG/PGT/PGR, UG/PGT graduates and visiting PGR, excluding PGR graduates. More stringent professional-body regulations take precedence.

evidence.quote:
Misuse of Artificial Intelligence 
 
Misuse of Artificial Intelligence is defined as the unauthorised or unacknowledged use of artificial intelligence 
tools to generate content for work submitted for assessment, unless explicit permission / guidance has been 
given to use them as part of the assessment method. Using GenAI tools such as ChatGPT to generate material 
for work submitted for assessment, without any form of editing or acknowledgement, or by not following the 
assessment guidelines fully, may constitute academic misconduct.

records.statement: Aberdeen’s academic discipline standard is the balance of probabilities: after reviewing available evidence, the decision-maker considers whether the event more likely than not occurred. University-level Investigating Officers come from a different School; an allegation can be upheld, not upheld or dismissed.

scope.audience: students
qualifiers: Code of Practice on Student Discipline (Academic) 2026/27, approved June 2026; currently registered UG/PGT/PGR, UG/PGT graduates and visiting PGR, excluding PGR graduates. More stringent professional-body regulations take precedence.

evidence.quote:
2.2 For cases that are being dealt with at University level, a n Investigating Officer will be selected from a 
list of academics approved by  Senate. The Investigating Officer will be from a different School from 
which the allegation has been raised. 
 
2.3 The standard of proof that shall be used in all cases under this Code is the balance of probabilities. This 
means that a Head of School, Investigating Officer or anyone else permitted to make a decision under 
this Code will be satisfied that an event occurred if they decide, having reviewed the evidence available,

2.4 The possible decisions an Investigation Officer can take when deciding if a case of alleged Academic
