records.statement: For minor undergraduate first cases, a professor may choose the pedagogical approach; repeat cases go to the regular process. A student can request appeal through the faculty vice-dean office within five working days of receiving the professor’s decision, moving into the disciplinary approach. The professor communicates a minor-case decision within five working days of the written allegation.

scope.audience: Students in the cited programme/course/stage only

evidence.quote:
A.4.3.1.1 A professor who suspects a student of having committed academic misconduct that the professor deems minor, as part of an individual or group assignment, may choose to address the matter using a pedagogical approach. (In case of doubt as to the seriousness of the offence, the professor may consult the dean or dean’s representative). If the infraction is minor, the professor will communicate their decision to the student within five (5) working days from the day the professor informs the student in writing of the allegation.
A-4.3.1.2 Depending on the nature of the case, a professor may determine that it be referred to the dean or dean’s representative who will handle it following the accelerated or regular process (see Disciplinary Approach).
A-4.3.1.3 As part of the pedagogical approach, the professor may impose one or more of the following sanctions:
Give a written warning.
Ask the student to participate in an AWHC workshop or another workshop on academic integrity. In this case, the student must provide proof of participation in the workshop.
Redo the assignment correctly.
Lower a work’s grade up to a maximum of 10% of the final course grade.
Any other measure considered appropriate for the circumstances.
A-4.3.1.4 The procedure for handling an academic misconduct allegation using the pedagogical approach involves five steps:
The professor contacts the office of the vice-dean or vice-dean’s representative to confirm that this is the student’s first case of academic misconduct; otherwise, the case must be handled using the regular process.
The professor contacts the student to discuss the allegation to better understand the reasons that led to academic misconduct and determine the most appropriate sanction.
Using the template provided, the professor informs the student of the sanction, as well as of the right to appeal. The professor also informs the vice-dean or vice-dean’s representative and the Faculty’s Office of Undergraduate Studies. The information related to the case will be kept in the student’s file.
The student accepts or appeals the sanction. If the sanction is appealed, the case will proceed using the disciplinary approach.
To appeal the sanction, the student must submit a written request to the office of the vice-dean or vice-dean’s representative of the faculty that offers the course, within five (5) working days of receiving the professor’s decision.

records.statement: Warwick Regulation 11 distinguishes misconduct involving intention to gain unfair advantage or knowledge the conduct may do so, from poor academic practice such as inadequate referencing without that intent.

scope.audience: students

evidence.quote:
A3 Academic Misconduct
A3.1 Definition
Academic misconduct are acts or omissions by a student which give or have the potential to give an unfair advantage in an examination or assessment, or might assist someone else to gain an unfair advantage, or an activity likely to undermine the integrity essential to scholarship and research. An advantage is unfair if it is, or intended to be, obtained by an act specifically disallowed in this Regulation, or if it goes against the principles of academic integrity underpinning this Regulation.
A3.2 Intention
Academic misconduct requires the intention to obtain an unfair advantage, or knowingly engaging in a behaviour that has the potential to give an unfair advantage, irrespective of whether such advantage is actually obtained.

A4 Poor Academic Practice
A4.1 Definition
Poor academic practice is the failure to observe principles of academic integrity. It typically (but not exclusively) occurs when referencing is inadequate, but not in a way suggesting that the student attempted to gain an unfair advantage.

A1 Scope
These regulations apply to students currently or previously registered on an award-bearing undergraduate or postgraduate taught course or research degree delivered by the University and those registered to study for the award of academic credit delivered by the University.

localSummary.zh: Warwick Reg11 区分学术违规与 poor academic practice：违规涉及取得不公平优势的意图或明知行为可能带来该优势；不良学术习惯常见于引用不足但没有试图获取不公平优势的情况。

records.statement: Poor academic practice receives no penalty deduction and is assessed by academic marking criteria. The no-appeal wording concerns that academic judgement, not loss of appeal rights after a misconduct finding or disciplinary sanction.

scope.audience: students

evidence.quote:
A4 Poor Academic Practice
A4.1 Definition
Poor academic practice is the failure to observe principles of academic integrity. It typically (but not exclusively) occurs when referencing is inadequate, but not in a way suggesting that the student attempted to gain an unfair advantage.
A4.2 Marking
There is no penalty for poor academic practice: marks are not deducted, instead work is assessed under the marking criteria (e.g., the University Marking Scales have an implicit expectation in respect of good academic practice).
A4.3 No appeals
Judgements about poor academic practice are academic judgements against which there is no appeal.

B5 Appeals
B5.1 Right to Appeal
The student has the right of appeal against either the decision of the Academic Integrity Panel or the sanction applied.
B5.2. Grounds of Appeal
Appeals may be made on the following grounds only:
(i) That there is evidence of a procedural irregularity in the conduct of the Panel.
(ii) That there is evidence of prejudice or bias on the part of the Panel.
(iii) That the student is in possession of relevant evidence which was not available to the Panel at the time of its decision. In this instance, the student must provide a reasonable explanation for why the evidence was not made available earlier.

A1 Scope
These regulations apply to students currently or previously registered on an award-bearing undergraduate or postgraduate taught course or research degree delivered by the University and those registered to study for the award of academic credit delivered by the University.

records.statement: Warwick’s 60 University working days for case handling and 30 for hearing appeals are indicative targets the University endeavours to meet. More preparation time or postponed meetings may be requested; these are not inflexible completion deadlines.

scope.audience: students

evidence.quote:
B2.2 Timeliness
The University recognises that investigations into alleged academic misconduct can be very stressful for students.
The University endeavours to meet the following indicative timeframes, unless the student requests additional time to make submissions or postponement of meeting during the process:
(i) The work of an Academic Conduct Panel and any subsequent meeting of an Academic Integrity Panel will be concluded within 60 University Working Days of an allegation being made to the student;
(ii) The student will be provided by the Academic Registrar with a statement of the allegations made against them, together with copies of any supporting evidence, at least five University Working Days before the meeting of Academic Integrity Panel.
(iii) An appeal will be heard within 30 University Working Days of the student making the appeal.

A1 Scope
These regulations apply to students currently or previously registered on an award-bearing undergraduate or postgraduate taught course or research degree delivered by the University and those registered to study for the award of academic credit delivered by the University.

B2.4 Representation
Throughout the academic integrity process, students will normally be expected to speak on their own behalf unless, for example, communication aids are required due to a disability.
In an Academic Conduct Panel, an Academic Integrity Panel, or Appeals Panel, a student may be accompanied by a person in a support capacity. This cannot be anyone who has been involved in relevant activities and would typically be a member of staff of the University, such as the student’s personal tutor or a senior tutor, a representative of the Student’s Union Advice Centre, a friend or family member. B2.5 Reasonable Adjustments
Reasonable adjustments to the processes described in the regulation, including the extension of deadlines for student responses, will be considered by the Chair of an Academic Conduct Panel or secretariat of an Academic Integrity Panel, and will be made where the student can provide relevant third party evidence that demonstrates the need for those adjustments.

(6) If the Academic Conduct Panel decides that, on the balance of probabilities, academic misconduct has occurred, it should make a report to the Head of Department, including a recommendation as to the appropriate sanction or for referral to an Academic Integrity Panel. The Head of Department will communicate their decision to the student in writing.

(1) The student may request, within ten University Working Days of being informed by the Head of Department of the sanction, that the case is considered by an Academic Integrity Panel. The student must provide evidence to the Head of Department of why they feel the sanction applied is unreasonable and following this, the Head of Department will make a report to the Academic Registrar.
(2) Following receipt of a report of suspected academic misconduct the Academic Registrar will determine if referral to an Academic Integrity Panel is appropriate, or if there is no case to answer.
(3) If referral to an Academic Integrity Panel is deemed appropriate the Academic Registrar will share a copy of the report with the student and invite them to attend a meeting of an Academic Integrity Panel and to provide a written response to the report in advance of the meeting. The meeting will still be held if the student chooses not to attend; if the student wishes to attend but is unable to, reasonable efforts will be made to reschedule the meeting to allow the student to attend. Meetings may be held in person or virtually.

A1 Scope

records.statement: B5 permits an appeal against an Academic Integrity Panel decision or sanction for procedural irregularity, bias or new evidence not before the original Panel with an explanation of why not provided earlier. The captured B5 text gives no filing-day count.

scope.audience: students

evidence.quote:
B5 Appeals
B5.1 Right to Appeal
The student has the right of appeal against either the decision of the Academic Integrity Panel or the sanction applied.
B5.2. Grounds of Appeal
Appeals may be made on the following grounds only:
(i) That there is evidence of a procedural irregularity in the conduct of the Panel.
(ii) That there is evidence of prejudice or bias on the part of the Panel.
(iii) That the student is in possession of relevant evidence which was not available to the Panel at the time of its decision. In this instance, the student must provide a reasonable explanation for why the evidence was not made available earlier.
B5.3 Appeal Review Panel stage
(1) An appeal will be considered by an Appeal Review Panel. The Appeal Review Panel will be constituted from one member drawn from the relevant Graduate Appeals Panel or the Undergraduate Appeals Panel and one of the following:
a) Chair of Faculty or their nominee
b) Chair or Deputy Chair of a Faculty Education and Student Experience Committee
c) Director of Graduate Studies or Director of Undergraduate Studies from a department other than that of the appellant.
No member of academic staff of any course or module studied by the appellant shall be a member of the Appeal Review Panel, nor should the Appeal Review Panel include any member of the appellant’s department.
(2) The Appeal Review Panel will consider whether an appellant has brought their appeal within the grounds as set out in B5.2 above and may also consider the substance and merits of the appeal and whether the factors advanced by the appellant would have had relevance at the time of the Academic Integrity Panel.
(3) The Appeal Review Panel must reject an appeal if it decides that:
(i) The student has not put forward any grounds for appeal, as laid down in B5.2.

(ii) For appeals on the basis that the student is in possession of relevant evidence which they were not able to present previously, the student has not put forward a reasonable explanation for the lack of availability of this evidence at the Academic Integrity Panel stage.
(4) Where the Appeal Review Panel considers that the evidence constitutes grounds for an appeal, the case will be referred to an Appeals Panel, constituted according to B3.4.

A1 Scope
These regulations apply to students currently or previously registered on an award-bearing undergraduate or postgraduate taught course or research degree delivered by the University and those registered to study for the award of academic credit delivered by the University.

evidence.quote:
Check the rules
The general position is that you can use Artificial Intelligence (AI) but must follow any requirements set out in assessments and course handbooks. Those requirements may restrict or prohibit the use of AI.
Read the assessment brief
Be sure to carefully read each assessment instructions to understand any specific requirements, restrictions, or prohibitions.
Keep a record
Record interactions with any AI that you later use or rely upon for a submission. This may be via screengrabs, or other recording techniques. Some assignments will have specific instructions around attaching any interactions, if that is the case, follow those instructions.
Protect privacy
Do not input any personal or confidential data into any AI tools, unless you fully understand what will happen to that data. The university recommends using Co-Pilot chat for this kind of data - when logged in with your Warwick account.
Declare it
You will be required to state if any AI has been used as part of the submission procedure.  If you use an AI, you must set out why, where and how you have done so - this may be done with a clear paragraph in your submission.
Reference AI
If you’re allowed to use AI, specific citation (referencing) requirements may be given to you as part of any assessment brief, if so, then follow those instructions.
Ask questions
If you’re unsure, please contact the tutor. It’s always better to check than to risk breaching academic integrity!

How to declare and reference AI in your assessments (if permitted)
If your assessment brief confirms that you're allowed to use AI tools or include AI generated content, you must follow those rules and acknowledge your AI use properly.
1. Declare your use of AI.
Include a short paragraph in your assignment submission explaining how you've used it. Check out some examples of AI disclosures on the AI Library GuideLink opens in a new window

Even if it's not required, always keep records just in case, and be prepared to share them with your tutor if you're asked. If you're unsure if you need to do this, check with your module tutor.

records.statement: Research guidance strongly advises against personal, confidential, third-party or business-critical input, with exceptional cases discussed individually. High-risk personal-data processing needs a DPIA; opt out of training where available. Patentable research must not be entered. These research conditions remain distinct from the student FAQ.

scope.audience: Researchers including research students
qualifiers: Only the captured source, version, audience and conditions; no exhaustive currency certification.

evidence.quote:
Data Protection
Researchers must exercise caution and adopt responsible practices when using AI tools and must be mindful of ethical and legal obligations under UK GDPR and other applicable laws and regulations. Training in the application of UK GDPR is offered by the University and should be engaged in by all Researchers.
The University strongly advises Researchers not to enter any personal, confidential, third-party, or business critical data / information / material into an AI tool. However, there may be exceptional circumstances where this is appropriate, and this would need to be discussed on a case-by-case basis. A DPIA (Data Protection Impact Assessment) is required by law by Researchers who plan to process personal data, where a type of processing is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals engaged by the research.
The following must also be considered:
AnonymisationPrivacyData SecurityIntellectual PropertyCopyrightPatentable Research
Anonymisation
Due to the large amounts of data being processed by AI tools, it is easy for Researchers inadvertently to use or reveal sensitive information hidden among anonymised data in the tool. Researchers should be careful only to input the amount of anonymised data they need for their research purposes to reduce the likelihood of any ‘linkage’ between datasets in the AI tool that could enable re-identification of subjects in anonymous data records.
Privacy
Researchers must review the privacy policy of the AI tool provider for any AI tool they use and the privacy settings of the tool to ensure compliance with relevant Data Protection regulations.
Researchers should check the AI providers’ terms and conditions regarding training of models. As AI models evolve, providers are adapting their terms and conditions to allow them to retain information entered into their products for model training purposes. Researchers must do their best to scrutinise the terms and conditions of the AI providers to understand their rights and any limitations. Some AI tools allow users to “opt out” of giving permission for content to be used to train the model. Wherever this is an option, Researchers must choose to opt out before entering any content into the tool.
Data Security
AI tools may be susceptible to cyberattacks, potentially exposing sensitive information to unauthorised users. Researchers must employ robust cybersecurity measures to protect data and systems, in line with the University’s guidance and must always check the security settings of the AI tool they are using, especially if entering data into an AI tool outside the UK.
Researchers must abide by the University’s information management policy framework Information Management Policy Framework and should contact the IDG Helpdesk to seek further advice if required.
Intellectual Property
There are Intellectual Property considerations when using AI tools because entering content into an AI tool, including confidential or third party-owned information, could be considered as publicly releasing that information. AI tools may retain the rights to use any content entered to train their model. Intellectual Property, including copyrighted material, can only be used to train an AI model if there is consent from the rights holder or if an exemption to copyright applies. However, due to the ongoing emergence of new AI tools, there is no clear-cut guidance on what counts as an exemption. The user terms of service for each AI tool should outline what rights are granted to developers regarding any content entered into that tool.
Wherever possible, Researchers should seek to avoid entering large quantities of Intellectual Property, including copyrighted material, generated from research into AI tools. This is particularly important for any Intellectual Property that is unpublished, commercially sensitive or potentially patentable.
Copyright
Researchers must ensure the necessary permissions are in place for them to input any data / information / material legally into an AI tool. Researchers must only enter third party content, including copyrighted material, into an AI tool when express permission is granted from the owner of that Intellectual Property, even if content is made available by licenses such as Creative Commons.
Patentable Research
If Researchers generate any research that may contain patentable subject matter, they must not enter this content into an AI tool.

records.statement: Researchers record AI processing in a Data Management Plan, retain use records and declare tools and purposes. Publications and research theses require disclosure of the tool and how it was used; researchers remain accountable and AI cannot be an author. These provisions do not license AI in taught assessments.

scope.audience: Researchers including research students
qualifiers: Only the captured source, version, audience and conditions; no exhaustive currency certification.

evidence.quote:
Research Data
Researchers must detail any use of AI tools in collecting, analysing or otherwise processing research data in a Data Management Plan. Researchers should explain the reasons for using particular AI tool(s), including an evaluation of the risks associated with using those tools.
Researchers must keep careful records of how they have used AI tools in their research and make sure that this use of AI and the specific tool used is explicitly declared. It is recommended that any sharing of research data generated using AI tools include information on the specific tool used, when the tool was used, and how content was generated, in order to promote reproducibility. Guidance on data sharing agreements should be sought from Research & Impact Services.
Researchers should specify the terms for reuse for any data that they deposit in a repository and consider including explicit information about how the data can be used by AI tools. When depositing data in a repository, Researchers should follow the guidelines of the repository for acknowledging the use of AI tools. Researchers using open-source data generated using AI tools must abide by any conditions for reuse specified for that material by the owner of the material.
Researchers using data governed by permission given by research participants must make sure that the use of the material with an AI tool is in line with the original consent given by the participants.
Publications
Authors are accountable for the accuracy, integrity and originality of their research outputs, such as publications, including any use of AI tools. Authors are fully responsible for the content of their manuscript, even those parts produced by an AI tool, and are thus liable for any breach of publication ethics, even if this happens inadvertently through the use of an AI tool.
Authors who use AI tools in writing a manuscript, producing images or graphical elements, or in the collection and analysis of data, must disclose how the AI tool was used, and which tool was used.
Researchers must take care to avoid plagiarism. Research outputs must be the authors’ own work, not presenting others’ work or output from AI tools without appropriate referencing. Individual journals and publishers may have specific requirements or guidelines relating to reporting the use of AI tools, and these must be followed where applicable.
AI tools cannot be listed as an author of a paper given the need for accountability; AI tools cannot meet the requirements for authorship as they cannot take responsibility for the submitted work.
The above guidance for research publications also applies to research theses and to material prepared for dissemination or presentation to workshop or conference audiences.

evidence.quote:
B4.4 Procedure in an Academic Integrity Panel
(1) The student may request, within ten University Working Days of being informed by the Head of Department of the sanction, that the case is considered by an Academic Integrity Panel. The student must provide evidence to the Head of Department of why they feel the sanction applied is unreasonable and following this, the Head of Department will make a report to the Academic Registrar.
(2) Following receipt of a report of suspected academic misconduct the Academic Registrar will determine if referral to an Academic Integrity Panel is appropriate, or if there is no case to answer.
(3) If referral to an Academic Integrity Panel is deemed appropriate the Academic Registrar will share a copy of the report with the student and invite them to attend a meeting of an Academic Integrity Panel and to provide a written response to the report in advance of the meeting. The meeting will still be held if the student chooses not to attend; if the student wishes to attend but is unable to, reasonable efforts will be made to reschedule the meeting to allow the student to attend. Meetings may be held in person or virtually.
(4) All the documents for the Academic Integrity Panel meeting will be sent to participants 5 days before the date of the meeting.
(5) The Head of Department of the module in which the student is suspected of academic misconduct will present the allegation and answer questions of the Academic Integrity Panel pertaining to the case.
(6) The student will be invited to reply to the allegation(s) and has the right to request attendees who can attest to a question of fact as a witness and to address them via the Chair. Character or, expert witnesses are not part of the process but the student may request the presence of someone in a supporting role.
(7) If the Academic Integrity Panel is satisfied that academic misconduct is proven it will determine the sanction taking into account any admission of academic misconduct by the student.
(8) If the Academic Integrity Panel is not satisfied that the academic misconduct is proven, the student will receive an outcome letter informing them of this and the matter will be closed.

evidence.quote:
B5 Appeals
B5.1 Right to Appeal
The student has the right of appeal against either the decision of the Academic Integrity Panel or the sanction applied.
B5.2. Grounds of Appeal
Appeals may be made on the following grounds only:
(i) That there is evidence of a procedural irregularity in the conduct of the Panel.
(ii) That there is evidence of prejudice or bias on the part of the Panel.
(iii) That the student is in possession of relevant evidence which was not available to the Panel at the time of its decision. In this instance, the student must provide a reasonable explanation for why the evidence was not made available earlier.

evidence.quote:
Academic integrity and generative AI
AI can help you learn but using it dishonestly can be a violation of academic policies. We strongly encourage all students to review the University of Guelph Statement on Artificial Intelligence Systems, ChatGPT, Academic Integrity.
Do not copy-paste GenAI text into your assignment without proper citation (if allowed at all).
Note: Students should reference the style guide used in their course to cite GenAI content properly.
Check your syllabus: Some instructors allow AI use with limits, others don’t.
Be transparent: If you used AI, say how (e.g., “Used ChatGPT to generate outline only”).
You are responsible for the content you share: For example, AI can’t be a journal co-author because it can’t take responsibility for content; only people can do that.
Remember: When in doubt, ask your instructor before using GenAI in your work. At the U of G acceptable use of AI is determined by the course instructor and may vary across disciplines, programs and types of assessments.

evidence.quote:
Data privacy and security
Before using generative AI, whether in a standalone app or inside familiar software, confirm what’s approved, what data is safe to share, and how your inputs may be stored or reused.
Avoid sharing personal info, login credentials, or unpublished work.
Never use or upload other people's content in a GenAI tool even if you are using a paid for or data protected version.
Free AI tools may use your inputs to train future models—check their terms of service and privacy policies closely and note where they contradict each other.
Use university-approved tools when possible.
Many digital tools and software already have AI integrated into their systems. Check these tools to see if AI has been integrated and, if so, review their data privacy policies.

scope.audience: Instructors and teaching assistants
qualifiers: Only the captured source, version, audience and conditions; no exhaustive currency certification.

evidence.quote:
Academic Integrity: Ensuring students are learning with integrity can be challenging in the age of AI. The calendar's existing academic misconduct provisions (Unauthorized Aids and Assistance) cover unauthorized use of AI. Being explicit about your expectations regarding AI use in individual assessments and having students declare sources and prompts for AI use can be helpful promoting a culture of integrity. Use of tools for detecting AI use are not approved at Guelph and cannot be used to support an allegation of a breach of academic integrity. Continue to talk with your students and consider ways of re-designing assessments that maximize learning while minimizing opportunities for integrity breaches. This question guide may be helpful for engaging in those conversations regarding suspected misuse of Generative AI.
Privacy and Data security: Student work that can identify, or reasonably be linked to, an individual student is personal information under Ontario's Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act (FIPPA) and must be handled accordingly. Information Security's Artificial Intelligence Acceptable Use Guideline (May 2026) notes that identifiable student work is confidential information and cannot be shared in public AI tools (e.g. ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini), whether the account is free or a paid personal one. Prompts in those tools have left the University's custody and may train someone's next model. If a teaching/assessment task needs an external tool, you should strip the prompt of any identifying information, ask Information Security to review the tool (if not previously reviewed; infosec@uoguelph.ca), or build the task so students enter their own work themselves (while offering them an opt-out).
Microsoft Copilot, signed in with your University single sign-on, can be used for student information. Authenticated Copilot runs inside the University's Microsoft environment with enterprise data protection (Copilot: Get Started). Faculty and staff use various tools for other purposes, such as drafting, brainstorming, summarizing public material, and that is fine; but do not share student information with third-party tools. For more information, please review the Information Security guidelines for differentiation among data types.
Using AI for assessment: Substantive academic evaluations should never be made independently by AI: a grade is a human decision at this University and Senate-approved grading procedures require the exercise of discretion by instructors. Where an AI tool assesses student work, it is important to be transparent with students about how the tool is being used and the role it plays in the assessment process. Clear communication can help ensure that students understand how their work is being assessed and reduce the likelihood of grade appeals relating to assessment (Methods and Criteria or Misapplication of an Academic Regulation or Procedure). If you move toward secured formats for assessments (e.g. invigilated exams), be sure to consider students registered with Student Accessibility Services, and that for some students AI is assistive technology.

evidence.quote:
As we head into the fall semester, the use of generative AI in courses continues to prompt many questions from instructors. In support of both instructors and students, we are sharing some general guidelines, aimed at aligning AI use in course design and delivery with current best practices and associated university policies. These guidelines update the recommendations currently posted on the OTL website (Provisional Recommendations for the Use of Generative AI, 2023) and will continue to evolve with changes to institutional policies, AI models, and best practices.
Top Four Guidelines:
Talk with your students are AI in the first week and for each assessment and learning activity. Explain how it will be used (or not) and why you are taking this approach in your course.
Substantive academic evaluations should never be made independently by AI: a grade is a human decision at this University and Senate-approved grading procedures require the exercise of discretion by instructors. Clear communication can reduce the likelihood of grade appeals related to assessment (Methods and Criteria or Misapplication of an Academic Regulation or Procedure).
Read your outline once more before the term starts and make sure you have explained your AI expectations for each assessment
Ask for help. The Office of Teaching and Learning (otl@uoguelph.ca) takes any teaching question about AI and has programming this fall to support you; the School of Continuing Studies (scs@uoguelph.ca) takes questions related to DE courses and the McLaughlin Library offers resources on AI literacy (How the Library Can Help; library@uoguelph.ca). Information Governance and Compliance can support questions about privacy risks, and CCS for security risk assessment.
Note that several colleges and departments have developed their own guidelines. Please inquire with your Associate Dean, Academic, or Chair/Director.
Detailed Guidelines
Authority for AI use: As an instructor, you determine whether and how AI is incorporated into your courses. You may prohibit it, permit it in specified ways or for some tasks, or require it. However, be aware of how usage differs across courses within a program as this may influence students’ understanding of what is expected or appropriate. In graduate courses and other graduate learning contexts, expectations should also be considered alongside relevant research and supervisory expectations.
How AI is used: Ultimately, how you incorporate student use of AI should be guided by course learning outcomes. For example, are you aiming to improve AI awareness, promote critical and responsible use of AI, or prepare students to use AI in an authentic workplace setting? Depending on the learning outcome you may or may not choose to incorporate AI. Review Teaching and AI resources or Tools for Allowable Uses of AI or contact otl@uoguelph.ca for support.
Talk with your students: Two findings recur in most surveys of student AI use: use is now nearly universal, and students themselves are uneasy about what the tools are doing to their learning. Please remember that most students want to talk about AI and their learning. Take the time to explain your approach to AI and how those decisions support their learning. Note the library guide, Introduction to GenAI for Students, introduces generative AI, and helps students make responsible decisions for AI use.
Setting Expectations: Differences among courses in AI usage can be confusing for students. Please use your course outline, CourseLink site, as well as in-class conversations to review and explain the expectations for using AI in your course (Course Outline Statements on AI). Articulate your expectations for each assessment as to how students should demonstrate their learning and acknowledge AI use. You may be unsure or uncomfortable about talking with your students about AI. If this is the case, please reach out to OTL (otl@uoguelph.ca) or the Library (How the Library Can Help, library@uoguelph.ca).
Academic Integrity: Ensuring students are learning with integrity can be challenging in the age of AI. The calendar's existing academic misconduct provisions (Unauthorized Aids and Assistance) cover unauthorized use of AI. Being explicit about your expectations regarding AI use in individual assessments and having students declare sources and prompts for AI use can be helpful promoting a culture of integrity. Use of tools for detecting AI use are not approved at Guelph and cannot be used to support an allegation of a breach of academic integrity. Continue to talk with your students and consider ways of re-designing assessments that maximize learning while minimizing opportunities for integrity breaches. This question guide may be helpful for engaging in those conversations regarding suspected misuse of Generative AI.
Privacy and Data security: Student work that can identify, or reasonably be linked to, an individual student is personal information under Ontario's Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act (FIPPA) and must be handled accordingly. Information Security's Artificial Intelligence Acceptable Use Guideline (May 2026) notes that identifiable student work is confidential information and cannot be shared in public AI tools (e.g. ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini), whether the account is free or a paid personal one. Prompts in those tools have left the University's custody and may train someone's next model. If a teaching/assessment task needs an external tool, you should strip the prompt of any identifying information, ask Information Security to review the tool (if not previously reviewed; infosec@uoguelph.ca), or build the task so students enter their own work themselves (while offering them an opt-out).
Microsoft Copilot, signed in with your University single sign-on, can be used for student information. Authenticated Copilot runs inside the University's Microsoft environment with enterprise data protection (Copilot: Get Started). Faculty and staff use various tools for other purposes, such as drafting, brainstorming, summarizing public material, and that is fine; but do not share student information with third-party tools. For more information, please review the Information Security guidelines for differentiation among data types.
Using AI for assessment: Substantive academic evaluations should never be made independently by AI: a grade is a human decision at this University and Senate-approved grading procedures require the exercise of discretion by instructors. Where an AI tool assesses student work, it is important to be transparent with students about how the tool is being used and the role it plays in the assessment process. Clear communication can help ensure that students understand how their work is being assessed and reduce the likelihood of grade appeals relating to assessment (Methods and Criteria or Misapplication of an Academic Regulation or Procedure). If you move toward secured formats for assessments (e.g. invigilated exams), be sure to consider students registered with Student Accessibility Services, and that for some students AI is assistive technology.
Use of 3rd party platforms. You may wish to have students use a 3rd party learning resource that uses AI. For platforms that are new to the university, confirm with the Office of Information Governance & Compliance, University Secretariat, that there are no privacy risks associated with the platform and CCS to ensure there are no security risks. Also, work with your College Dean or designate to ensure you are complying with the Ancillary Fees policy, which requires their use to be clearly communicated in the course outline, assessments conducted to constitute no more than 30% of the final grade, cost to be reasonable, and where feasible offer an alternative learning resource or grading scheme for students experiencing financial hardship.

Date: September 30, 2024

Subject: Use of GenAI detection tools and recommendations if you suspect academic
misconduct related to GenAI
_____________________________________________________________________________________

This message is intended for ADAs, Chairs, and Directors, and contains relevant information for all
course instructors and teaching assistants as they navigate student use of Generative AI (GenAI).

Currently, the university has not authorized the use of GenAI detection tools for the detection and
prosecution of academic misconduct. The reasons behind this decision can be found in the
Provisional Recommendations for the Use of Generative AI in teaching, published by the Office of
Teaching and Learning.

Article 8 of the Provisional Recommendations provides the following:

8. Generative AI plagiarism detection software is not currently approved for use at UofG. This
   software will continue to be reviewed and may be available in the future.
   a. Many of these detectors will produce false positives or negatives (see also McCrosky, 2024
       and Weber-Wulff et al., 2023), and their use may constitute an infringement upon the
       students’ privacy or intellectual property rights. In many cases, it is unclear how the
       material submitted to third-party detectors is retained or used.
   b. Until more is understood about generative AI detection tools, instructors should not submit
       student work to generative AI detection tools. (Please note that this is different from
       submitting student work to generative AI tools – for example, to get AI-generated feedback –
       as noted in recommendation 7(h) above.)
   c. UofG has an institutional subscription to Turnitin, a plagiarism detection software.
       Turnitin announced an update aimed at detecting writing produced by generative AI, which
       has brought about a variety of concerns. UofG, like many other institutions, has not yet
       turned on this feature as there is a need to understand the functionality of the tool, assess
       the security and privacy considerations for student work, and determine whether it aligns
       with existing policies.

records.statement: The May 2026 guide distinguishes directly AI-generated text/images/translations from editorial suggestions on student-authored work. Generated material must still be identified after editing. A required honour declaration does not replace proper referencing, and each subject/assessment’s restrictions control.

scope.audience: Students in the cited programme/course/stage only
qualifiers: Only the captured source, version, audience and conditions; no exhaustive currency certification.

evidence.quote:
1.   The work that you submit for assessment must be YOUR OWN WORK. This means that the
     work must be original in the sense that it is your intellectual creation and its overall content is
     representative of your own expression of your own ideas, not a copy/version of other people’s
     work or AI-generated material. Asking GenAI to do the assignment for you is like asking
     someone else to do the assignment for you, and copying AI-generated content is like copying
     other people’s work. Both are cheating and are penalisable.

2.   AI-generated material refers to any text, images, or translations created directly by an AI tool at
     prompt or otherwise (and not editorial suggestions, corrections and refinements made by AI on
     content that you have authored). Such material should be identified as AI-generated no matter
     how much you have edited it afterwards. If you use AI-generated materials in any part of your
     work, you must reference them in accordance with the accepted academic conventions (e.g. APA
     or MLA styles) like you would have referenced other people’s work. Beware that AI-generated
     contents can sometimes contain material that breaches copyright, and you may infringe the
     copyright law unintentionally by incorporating such material in your work.

3.   Some subjects and assessments may not allow or have restrictions on the use of GenAI tools.
     You may be required to declare the use of GenAI tools (e.g. by completing an honour declaration
     form) and identify the AI-generated content in your work. You should refer to the relevant
     subject and assessment documents for the specific restrictions and requirements. It should be

M365 Copilot Chat, M365 Copilot, and Copilot Studio
Microsoft recently released M365 Copilot Chat, M365 Copilot, and Copilot Studio to higher education institutions through the Education program offer. If you plan to leverage these tools, please be aware of the differences in functionalities and the licensing / usage fees involved.
M365 Copilot Chat
M365 Copilot Chat replaces Copilot with Bing and supports text-to-text messaging, along with the ability to upload files or images for text conversion.
All PolyU staff and students can leverage M365 Copilot Chat via the PolyU Gen AI app, or by accessing it directly through the browser at https://www.microsoft365.com/chat. Users can also install the Microsoft 365 Copilot app on their personal mobile phones. M365 Copilot Chat utilizes the Microsoft Prometheus model, which is built upon OpenAI's GPT-4o.
M365 Copilot
Microsoft 365 Copilot is relevant to those who like to have personal AI Assistant to manage own email messages on O365 and documents saved on O365 OneDrive. M365 Copilot integrates with Microsoft 365 applications (MS Team, Outlook, MS Word, Excel & PowerPoint) to ease document and PowerPoint creation, content summarization, Excel data analysis and summarize email threats. M365 Copilot is not included in the standard Education license subscription and requires the purchase of an additional M365 Copilot subscription license for use.
Copilot Studio
Copilot Studio is for colleagues who want to build their own AI chatbots using data from the O365 Graph or the Internet. The use of Copilot Studio requires the purchase of a Copilot Studio subscription license. If the AI chatbot will be used by others, the creator of the AI chatbot needs to purchase conversation minutes to allow others to make conversation with the AI chatbot created.
If you need further information or assistance, please contact the IT HelpCentre (Tel: 2766 5900, WhatsApp/ WeChat: 6577 9669) or reach out to us via the IT Online ServiceDesk.

The April 2026 announcement says all TMU Google-account holders can access NotebookLM. These public conditions were reviewed; no personal account activation or student entitlement was tested.

evidence.quote:
The Google Gemini App (“Gemini”) and NotebookLM are conversational generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools that process information and respond to prompts you provide. While both tools are available to TMU employees and students, they serve different purposes: Gemini is designed for open-ended brainstorming and web-based research, while NotebookLM is grounded specifically in the documents you provide.
Both tools can be used to:
Assist with writing tasks
Summarize documents
Repurpose content for various uses
Support brainstorming and idea-generation
Create resources in various formats, including image, audio and video
TMU's access to the Gemini App and NotebookLM are a safer alternative to other GenAI tools such as ChatGPT or Microsoft Copilot, as it is covered by our Google Workspace for Education Terms of Service (external link) . Your activities will not be used to train Gemini's AI models.
Please note that some functionality is only available to users 18 years of age and older.
Protect TMU data by only using public or low-sensitivity information with Google Gemini. Sensitive and confidential information should never be used in prompts, attached files, or other activities in Gemini.
Copyrighted material and the intellectual property of others should never be used as source materials without consent from the copyright holders.
Gemini's responses are likely to have inaccuracies. You are responsible for reviewing and correcting them before using or sharing them with others.
Begin your journey with (google doc) Generative AI Literacy (external link) and building your (google doc) prompt writing (external link) skills. These are crucial to getting good outputs from generative AI.
About Google's generative AI tools
Unlike a search engine that provides a list of existing websites, these tools use language patterns to build entirely new, conversational answers to your specific instructions. TMU provides access to two options: the Gemini App for open-ended exploration and NotebookLM for focused work with your own documents.
The Gemini App is an ideal tool for brainstorming about broad topics because it creates responses using information from across the public web. In contrast, NotebookLM acts as a focused assistant that helps you find details and make connections using only the specific files and links you choose to provide.
Like other large language models (LLMs) this system can make mistakes, and you are unlikely to get the exact same result twice.
Open All Close All
How do I access Google's AI tools?
After logging into your TMU account, you can access the tools through the following web addresses:
gemini.google.com (external link)
notebooklm.google.com (external link)
You can also access these tools by clicking the Google Apps button in the upper right-hand corner of your TMU Gmail account. Your TMU account should be visible in the upper-right corner upon opening NotebookLM.
By using your TMU account, you can ensure that your data will not be used to train Google's AI models.

Google NotebookLM is now available for all TMU Google accounts
April 28, 2026
To: All faculty and staff
All TMU Google account holders can now use their university Google Workspace account to access the education version of Google NotebookLM, an artificial intelligence (AI) tool designed for analysis, content organization and note-taking.
While the Google Gemini app (external link) (which became available at TMU a year ago) serves as a general prompt-based assistant using publicly-available information from the internet, NotebookLM is designed to work with files and data of your choice.
Key features of NotebookLM
Targeted analysis: You can upload or select specific files from your TMU Google Drive (such as documents, PDFs or videos) or link to websites. NotebookLM only analyzes these selected materials to summarize information, create study guides and answer questions with citations.
Collaboration: The "notebooks" you create in NotebookLM can be shared. You can grant others viewer or editor access to contribute to the sources used and generate content.
You can access the tool at notebooklm.google.com (external link) or by clicking the Google apps button in the upper right hand corner of your TMU Gmail account. Your TMU account should be visible in the upper right corner upon opening NotebookLM.
Protecting TMU data

evidence.quote:
How your data is protected in Google's AI tools
Open All Close All
How does Google protect my data?
When accessing the Gemini App or NotebookLM using your TMU account, your data is not used or human-reviewed to improve AI models. This feature is covered by the Google Workspace for Education Terms of Service (external link) .
Keep in mind that access to a Google Gemini or NotebookLM account outside of TMU does not fall under these terms of service and therefore any data you enter in an account outside of TMU is subject to review or could be used to improve their AI models.
We recommend that you always confirm you are accessing Gemini or NotebookLM from your TMU account each time you begin a new prompt by clicking your profile picture in the top-right corner. You’ll want this to show your @torontomu.ca email address instead of your personal one. By using your TMU account, you can ensure that your data will not be used to train Google's AI models.
Prior to the release of the Gemini App and NotebookLM at TMU, we conducted privacy and AI impact assessments with the Office of the General Counsel and Board Secretariat, and a security risk assessment with the Office of the Chief Information Security Officer.
Can others at TMU view my prompt history and activities?
Although your activities in the Gemini App and NotebookLM are not public, TMU's Google administrators in Computing and Communications Services (CCS) can view prompt histories in the Gemini App, but not in NotebookLM. Our administrators cannot access any files you upload to either Gemini or NotebookLM. For more on how the university’s technologies are monitored, please visit TMU's Student Computing Guidelines under the "Privacy" section (for students) and TMU’s Electronic Monitoring Policy (for employees).
Responsible use guidelines
Open All Close All
What information is appropriate to share with TMU's Google AI tools?
Each person is responsible for ensuring they don't share inappropriate information with TMU's Google AI tools.
Only public or low-sensitivity information should be input to these tools. Sensitive and confidential information should never be used in prompts, uploaded files or other activities. For help defining what is considered sensitive information, please review TMU’s Information Classification Standard and Handling Guidelines.
Do not upload, input or share any personal information about yourself or any TMU student, faculty or staff member into Google's AI tools. Examples of personal information include any data that is personally identifiable such as protected health information, social insurance numbers, student/staff numbers, birthdates, credit card data, etc. Failure to abide by this guidance may result in a privacy breach and/or non-compliance with privacy legislation.
It isn't appropriate to share copyrighted information nor the intellectual property of others with Google's AI tools, including your students' work and resources provided through the TMU Libraries.

evidence.quote:
6.3. Notification to student
6.3.1. Students must be notified of a suspicion of academic misconduct in a confidential and timely manner. The notification occurs as part of the registration process and will include an invitation for the opportunity to discuss the matter with the decision maker. Concerns about academic misconduct should be discussed during the scheduled FD/NFD rather than in advance or outside of the formal process. (See Procedures, Sections 1 and 2)
6.3.2. Any evidence that can be shared in advance of the discussion will be made available to the student. While every effort will be made to provide as much information as possible in advance, additional evidence may be presented to the student at the discussion.
6.3.3. Students may not drop a course in which there is a suspicion of academic misconduct. At the start of the process, the Registrar’s Office, will place a DEF on the student’s academic record for the course in which there is an active investigation. If the student drops the course before the DEF is placed, the RO will re-enroll the student. (See Procedures, Section 5)
6.4. Discussion (FD/NFD)
6.4.1. The purpose of a discussion is to allow the decision maker to present the basis for their suspicion and for the student(s) to offer their perspective and answer questions. Discussions are to be carried out in a spirit of inquiry, rather than in an accusatory or adversarial manner. The discussion is a continuation of the preliminary investigation and therefore may result in changes to the nature of the suspected academic misconduct (e.g., the initial suspicion indicated “plagiarism” but the discussion clarified that what had actually occurred was “contract cheating”).
6.4.1.1. If, during an NFD, either party fails to engage in a respectful manner, either party may choose to terminate the discussion and request an FD.
6.4.1.2. If, during an FD, either party fails to engage in respectful manner, the facilitator will intervene.
6.4.2. At a discussion, the decision maker, the student(s) suspected of academic misconduct, and the facilitator (for an FD) will be present. When appropriate, other parties may be present (see Section 11).
6.4.3. No decisions related to the suspected academic misconduct should be made prior to the discussion nor should any decision be communicated during the discussion.
6.4.4. If a student fails to attend the discussion and fails to notify the AIO within 24 hours of the scheduled meeting to provide a reasonable explanation for their absence, the decision maker may proceed without the student’s input. If the decision maker fails to attend the discussion and fails to notify the AIO within 24 hours of the scheduled meeting to provide a reasonable explanation for their absence, the matter will be dismissed. The AIO may make exceptions due to extenuating circumstances.
6.4.5. Discussions are not to be audio or video recorded. A written record of the meeting will be maintained. With the permission of all parties, a university approved transcription tool may be used to create the written record.
In the case of FDs, the AIO will create the record and issue a copy to the student and decision maker.

evidence.quote:
11. Appeals and Penalty Hearings
11.1. Students must appeal first to the AIC, RAC or GAAC (as appropriate) and may only appeal further to the SAC on the grounds provided in Policy, Section 14.1 , with the exception of appeals relating to a recommendation of a DW or expulsion, where the student can waive the first level hearing and go directly to SAC.
11.2. Hearings are not open to the public due to privacy and confidentiality issues.
11.3. Hearings are not to be audio or video recorded. No minutes are taken. The decision letter is the only official record of the hearing.
12. Appeals - General Regulations
12.1. Appeals are initiated by students.
12.2. Students have ten (10) business days from the date of issue of the decision letter to submit an appeal to the AIC/RAC/GAAC.
12.2.1. If an appeal is not filed by the deadline, the decision will stand. Where mitigating circumstances exist, and appropriate supporting documentation is provided, the Director of the AIO (or designate, for the AIO), the Registrar (or designate, for the RAC), the Vice-Provost and Dean YSGPS (or designate for the GAAC) or the Secretary of Senate (or designate, for the SAC) may accept a late appeal.
12.3. In specified circumstances a further appeal may be made to the SAC (See Policy Section 14). Students have ten (10) business days from the date of issue of the appeal decision letter to submit an appeal to the SAC.
12.4. Where a full appeal hearing is to be held, if the student fails to attend, the appeal will be withdrawn and no further appeals will be accepted. Where mitigating circumstances exist, and appropriate supporting documentation is provided, the Director of the AIO (or designate for the AIC) , the Registrar (or designate for the RAC), the Vice-Provost and Dean YSGPS (or designate for the GAAC) or the Secretary of Senate (or designate for the SAC) have discretion to reschedule the hearing.
12.5. Students may remain in class and may enroll in courses while their case is under appeal. However, if the assigned penalty is removal from placement, co-op program option, internship, or practicum, the student may not remain in the associated course(s) during the appeal process.

تکنواسترس: چالشی نوظهور در عصر یادگیری هوش مصنوعی در میان اعضای هیئت علمی دانشگاه
نوع مقاله : مقاله پژوهشی

استاد، گروه آموزش علوم تربیتی، دانشگاه تبریز

چکیده
هدف: پیشرفت‌های سریع فناوری‌های مبتنی بر هوش مصنوعی در آموزش عالی، ضمن ایجاد فرصت‌های نوین، چالش‌هایی همچون تکنواسترس را برای اساتید دانشگاه به همراه داشته است. هدف این پژوهش، بررسی کیفی تجربه اساتید دانشگاه از تکنواسترس در عصر هوش مصنوعی است.
روش‌شناسی‌: پژوهش حاضر از نوع کیفی و با رویکرد پدیدارشناسی تفسیری انجام شد. شرکت‌کنندگان شامل 21 استاد از دانشگاه‌های تبریز و دانشگاه فرهنگیان تبریز بودند که با روش نمونه‌گیری هدفمند انتخاب شدند. داده‌ها از طریق مصاحبه نیمه ساختاریافته جمع‌آوری و با روش هفت مرحله ای کلایزی تحلیل گردید. اعتبار یافته‌ها با استفاده از شاخص‌های قابلیت اعتبار، انتقال‌پذیری، اعتمادپذیری و تأییدپذیری صورت گرفت.
یافته‌ها: تحلیل داده‌ها چهار تم اصلی شامل عوامل زمینه‌ساز تکنواسترس (ابعاد فردی-روانشناختی، آموزشی-سازمانی، ماهیت فناوری و هنجارهای محیطی-اجتماعی)؛ پیامدها و تبعات (تضعیف عملکرد آموزشی-پژوهشی، تهدید کیفیت زندگی حرفه‌ای و چالش‌های روان‌شناختی)؛ رشد حرفه‌ای و سازگاری اساتید در مواجهه با تکنواسترس (نوآوری در تدریس، توسعه مهارت‌های دیجیتال، بهبود فرصت‌های پژوهشی و افزایش انعطاف‌پذیری) و راهبردهای مقابله‌ای (راهبردهای فردی، حمایت سازمانی و سیاست‌گذاری‌ و برنامه‌ریزی) را آشکار ساخت.
نتایج: علیرغم دیدگاه‌های متفاوت درباره ماهیت مثبت یا منفی تکنو استرس، این پدیده می‌تواند بر سلامت روان، کیفیت زندگی حرفه‌ای و بهره‌وری علمی اعضای هیئت علمی اثرگذار باشد. و علاوه بر پیامدهای منفی، فرصتی برای رشد حرفه‌ای، نوآوری آموزشی و توسعه مهارت‌های دیجیتال نیز فراهم می‌کند.

evidence.quote:
Purpose 
This policy sets out the University of Liverpool’s requirements for the use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in learning, teaching and assessment.  
It establishes a clear institutional baseline for responsible use, transparency, academic integrity, accessibility, data protection, copyright and governance, while supporting AI literacy and assessment design that prepares students for further study, work and global citizenship in an AI enabled world. 
Scope 
This policy applies to all students and staff engaged in learning, teaching, and assessment. 
It should be read alongside the Code of Practice on Assessment (including the Academic Integrity Policy), the University’s data protection and accessibility requirements, and any approved programme, School, Department or Professional, Statutory and Regulatory Body requirements that are more restrictive. 
The appropriate use of GenAI varies by discipline and professional context. Schools, Departments, programme teams and relevant PSRBs may set more restrictive expectations than this institutional baseline, and where such requirements exist, they must be followed. 
Medical, clinical and other professionally regulated programmes may have additional obligations, including Fitness to Practice, patient safety and PSRB requirements. In these contexts, programme teams must ensure that generative AI use and tier decisions remain consistent with those obligations. 
Principles 
Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) must not replace a student’s own thinking or work or be used in ways that misrepresent what the student can do.
Use of GenAI must be lawful, ethical, inclusive, and proportionate. Students must understand that GenAI outputs may be inaccurate, biased, incomplete, or misleading, and must always exercise critical judgement. 
The University will support students and staff to develop GenAI literacy so that GenAI can be used critically, effectively, ethically, and transparently in academic work and professional practice, including the ability to select appropriate tools and agents for specific learning, teaching, assessment, and professional tasks. 
Students must declare or acknowledge use where required by the assessment, local guidance or University requirements. 

Assessment requirements 
All assessments must state clearly whether, and to what extent, generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) may be used. 
When setting these requirements, staff will use the University’s approved tiered framework for GenAI permissions in assessment (Table 1: 4.7). 
Where the applicable GenAI tier is not explicitly stated for an assessment, the default permission will be Tier 2, except for invigilated exams, which will default to Tier 1, in line with the approved framework.
For each assessment, Canvas (or an equivalent alternative where Canvas is not used) will clearly state the applicable permissions-framework tier and any associated permissions or restrictions, so students understand what is permitted, restricted, or prohibited
Students must satisfy the requirements set for each assessment. Use of GenAI beyond the stated requirements would normally constitute academic misconduct.

evidence.quote:
1 
Prohibited: No AI use 
No GenAI use (including basic tools such as grammar checkers), unless required under an approved student support plan. Enforced via supervision or controlled conditions. Aims to test unaided skills and knowledge. 
Must declare GenAI use in line with local guidance and the assessment brief. A record of approved adjustments for students with a support plan will be available to staff, and students will not need to declare the use of assistive technology.
2 
Contextual support: Limited / Assistive use 
GenAI is permitted in restricted and specified ways (e.g. for planning, editing, or support tasks only). GenAI is not central to demonstrating core learning outcomes; it is a tool to aid learning. 
Must declare GenAI use in line with local guidance and the assessment brief. 
3 
Structural scaffold: exploratory/ critical use 
In addition to Tier 2, GenAI use is broadly allowed and encouraged for specific stages or tasks. Students actively engage with AI (for example, generate, critique, iterate, refine) to build AI literacy without making AI the primary producer. 
Assessment guidance to include what evidence is required, e.g. could include a record of key AI interactions (such as a summary account of how AI was used, prompts, outputs, edits); critically evaluate AI contributions and cite or attribute use where appropriate.   
4 
Integrated: Integral / Embedded use 
In addition to Tiers 2 and 3, GenAI is a required or core element of the assessment. AI use is expected to achieve the learning outcomes with a focus on responsible, effective and ethical application. 

Assessment guidance to include what evidence is required, e.g. could include full transparency (for example, documenting process and prompts); reflect on ethical implications, biases, and accuracy; and demonstrate how human input adds value.

records.statement: Personal, sensitive, confidential, unpublished or restricted information must not enter public/consumer AI. University-data activity must use approved environments with University credentials; approval does not waive copyright, licence or professional obligations. Research and thesis activity also follows research-integrity and ethics guidance.

scope.audience: Students and staff handling University-related information
qualifiers: Only the captured source, version, audience and conditions; no exhaustive currency certification.

evidence.quote:
Data protection and confidentiality 
Any use of generative AI must comply with UK General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the University’s data protection requirements. Personal, sensitive, confidential, unpublished or otherwise restricted information must not be entered into public or consumer AI tools. 
Where proposed use involves University data, personal data or system integration, students must follow the University’s approved security, procurement and data protection processes, including completion of a Data Protection Impact Assessment where required. 
Research and thesis activity must also comply with the University’s research integrity, ethics and generative artificial intelligence-in-research guidance, including requirements on research data governance. 
Copyright and intellectual property 
Materials that are copyrighted, licensed, unpublished, or otherwise protected must not be uploaded to generative AI tools without appropriate permission, licence, or other lawful basis. This includes teaching materials, student work, unpublished research outputs, and subscription content.
Use of University-approved systems does not remove the requirement to comply with copyright, licensing, contractual or professional obligations. 
Accessibility and inclusive practice 
The University will take an inclusive approach to learning, teaching and assessment and will make reasonable adjustments where required for students with a disability, in line with institutional policy and the Equality Act 2010. 
Some students with a disability may use assistive technologies, including tools with AI-enabled functions, as part of approved reasonable adjustments.
The use of AI-enabled assistive technologies must remain consistent with assessment conditions, including the applicable GenAI tier, and with the University’s academic integrity requirements. 
In designing teaching and assessment, unnecessary barriers should be reduced through inclusive design, clear expectations, and proportionate support. 



Use of University approved AI tools’ 
For any University-related activity that involves University data, only University-approved AI environments must be used, and they must be accessed via University credentials with the appropriate institutional protections enabled. 
AI-enabled tools must not be procured, adopted or integrated for University purposes outside approved University processes.

evidence.quote:
Our M365 Copilot Proof of Concept trials
As part of the Liverpool 2031 vision and our wider digital transformation programme, the University has been working with Microsoft to explore how Copilot could add value for staff and academic activity.
First PoC (October 2025 – January 2026)
Our initial PoC involved colleagues from Education, Professional Services and Research. Participants were given paid Copilot licences for three months to test how the tool could support productivity, simplify workflows and enhance academic work.
Second PoC (April 2026 – November 2026)
Building on what we learned, a second, extended M365 Copilot PoC is now underway. This trial continues our exploration of Copilot, taking forward insights from the first PoC and testing the tool in more depth and across a more targeted range of use cases.
Feedback from this phase will help shape future decisions about AI tools, guidance and targeted pilots across the University.
To find out more about the M365 Copilot PoC trials, please contact copilot@liverpool.ac.uk.
Did you know?
You don’t need a full paid licence to start using Copilot today. Copilot Chat is available for free and can be used to ask questions, explore ideas, draft content documents, summarise text, get support with planning, brainstorming or quick research tasks.
While Copilot Chat doesn’t connect to institutional data in the same way the full M365 version does, it still offers powerful support for standalone tasks.
All University of Liverpool staff can access Copilot Chat via the icon at the top right of Microsoft Edge on your MWS device and more information can be found via our FAQ and Resource links below.

evidence.quote:
Is the use of AI tools considered to be academic misconduct at UBC?
At this time, whether the use of AI tools in courses and assessments is or is not allowed is a course or program-level decision.
Individual instructors must clarify expectations with their students in their syllabus according to updates to Senate Policies V-130 (Vancouver) and O-130 (Okanagan). Starting September 1, 2026 all syllabi must include a statement on the usage of generative AI tools as well as an academic integrity statement (Vancouver and Okanagan).
If instructors have questions about any Department or program level policies on artificial intelligence tools, they should reach out to their Department or program.
Students should review the guidelines established for their courses, make sure they have permission from their instructors before using any AI tools for assessed work, and ask their instructors if they have any questions or anything is unclear.
In general:
If using generative AI tools on coursework has been prohibited by the instructor, then using these tools to complete assignments or assessments would be considered academic misconduct.
If using generative AI tools has been permitted by the instructor, then instructors should make sure to convey the limitations of use and how it should be acknowledged and students’ use should stay within those bounds.
If the use of generative AI tools has not been discussed or specified by the instructor on the syllabus, then students should reach out to their instructor for clarification and permission for use.
Students should not assume that all available technologies are permitted. Students should be aware that AI is integrated into many technologies such as translation tools, writing and citation tools, and general search engines.
If students are not sure about whether AI tools are allowed, and for what stages of their work, as with any tool, they must ask their instructor for clarity and guidance.

          student-submitted work that clarifies how the use of GenAI is permitted
          or not permitted.

evidence.quote:
Can or should instructors use AI detectors to detect the use of AI tools on assignments or assessments?
The use of applications to detect AI-generated content is strongly discouraged at this time, due to concerns about effectiveness, accuracy, bias, privacy, and intellectual property.
Instructors should not submit student academic work or personal information to AI detectors that have not undergone a UBC Privacy Impact Assessment (PIA) and have not been approved for this use. As of Fall 2026, no AI detection tools have undergone a UBC PIA. The AI in Teaching and Learning website has a webpage on the current status of PIAs for generative AI tools at UBC.
UBC continues to assess the results of independent academic research into the effectiveness of AI detection tools, rather than relying on the statements from vendors that claim universally high accuracy. In general, detectors cannot keep pace with the rapid advances in model capability and the metrics used to ‘detect’ AI writing can be strongly biased against non-native English speakers. The announcement about UBC’s decision not to enable the AI detection feature in Turnitin provides further information about concerns with AI detectors.
Not using AI detectors does not mean giving up on academic integrity. There are things instructors can do proactively and responsively to encourage ethical and transparent use of AI tools in their classes and promote academic integrity. Instead of AI detectors, some of the approaches to evaluating possible academic misconduct that educators have used before the broad availability of GenAI may also be effective when considering inappropriate use of GenAI. These include comparing work produced out of out of class to work produced in class, or having an exploratory conversation with students about their work.
For more information about AI detection, please see Low-effort Strategies for Academic Integrity in the Age of GenAI (CTL).
If an instructor suspects that an assignment or assessment has been completed with unauthorized use of AI tools, they should proceed as they would for any other potential allegation of academic misconduct. An overview of the academic misconduct process for instructors is available on the academic integrity website.
Can instructors use Turnitin’s AI-detection feature in their courses?
Turnitin is a plagiarism prevention-tool available that helps check the academic integrity of student writing. Currently Turnitin’s AI-detection functionality is not available for use in any UBC course. In 2023, UBC reaffirmed their decision to not enable Turnitin’s new AI-detection feature.
On April 4 2023, Turnitin activated a new and separate feature that attempts to identify AI-generated text. The LT Hub Leadership group, with the support of the Provosts at both UBC Vancouver and UBC Okanagan, made the decision not to enable this feature at that time (April 2023) and has reaffirmed their decision (August 2023).
UBC is continuing to wait before deploying any AI-detection features, including the one by Turnitin, as more information is needed about the feature’s effectiveness, accuracy and bias mitigation, and about the ability to employ an AI detector as a robust component of talking to students about suspected academic misconduct. The use of other AI detection tools is also not recommended, due to similar issues as those noted above, as well as privacy and security concerns. To date, no AI detection tool has undergone a UBC Privacy Impact Assessment process.
What should instructors do if they suspect the unauthorized use of AI tools?
Instructors who suspect that a student has used generative artificial intelligence tools contrary to expectations should follow the standard academic misconduct process as they would for any misconduct allegation. This might include inviting the student in for a conversation about their work and any irregularities or inconsistencies identified.
If instructors have questions about their Faculty’s process, they should contact their Faculty delegate.
If students have concerns about any allegations of academic misconduct against them, they can reach out to the Office of the Ombudsperson for Students, AMS Advocacy, GSS Advocacy or SUO Advocacy.
