evidence.quote:
Diese Nutzungsbedingungen werden regelmäßig überprüft und weiterentwickelt. Änderungen werden rechtzeitig bekannt gegeben.
Terms of Use for OpenWebUI for Generative AI Systems at the University of Freiburg
These terms of use regulate the permissible use of the Open WebUI tool and the local and external AI models connected via this tool. The goal is to ensure a legally secure, responsible, and sustainable use of AI systems at the University of Freiburg. These terms of use concretize the "Directive on the Use and Operation of AI Systems at the Albert Ludwig University of Freiburg" (AI Directive*) for the specific system Open WebUI. The AI Directive remains unaffected and takes precedence in the event of contradictions.
Open WebUI is a supportive work tool. It does not replace professional, legal, or organizational decisions and is not designed as an autonomous specialist procedure or agentic system. All users are required to comply with the specified guidelines and notices to ensure a legally secure and ethically acceptable use of Open WebUI.
* The AI Directive is currently (as of July 2026) in the university's committee process and will enter into force upon its publication.
I. Mandatory AI Training
Before first use of Open WebUI, all users are required to complete the training course "Basics of AI: Understanding and Applying Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI)" available on the ILIAS learning platform.
The training serves to acquire the required AI competence as defined by the AI Directive. Further training requirements are governed by the AI Directive.
II. Principles of Using OpenWebUI
These terms of use regulate the use of the Open WebUI tool provided by the University of Freiburg, particularly the handling of inputs and outputs. Input refers to all user inputs, such as texts, documents, tables, images, or audio recordings. Output refers to the results generated by the connected AI models.
The responsibility for entered content and for the use of the generated results lies with the user. Results must be independently checked for factual accuracy, completeness, legal permissibility, and potential discriminatory effects. Generative AI can produce erroneous or biased content (hallucinations). Results must not be adopted without review or used as the sole basis for decision-making.
The use of Open WebUI is generally permitted, provided that the legal requirements, in particular data protection, copyright, and higher education law, as well as the provisions of the AI Directive of the University of Freiburg, are complied with and no prohibited AI practices within the meaning of the AI Regulation exist. The usage scenarios documented in Annex 1 represent reviewed and approved standard applications. They serve as guidance and concretize typical use cases in research, teaching, and administration.
A brief overview of the most important rules for use ("What am I allowed to do, what am I not allowed to do") can also be found in the usage scenarios (Annex 1) and in the short guide (Annex 2).
Other use cases are also permitted without separate approval if they comply with the legal requirements and do not give rise to increased risk within the meaning of these terms of use. In case of doubt, prior consultation with the responsible AI contact person in accordance with § 9 para. 3 of the AI Directive is required.
Use cases with increased risk
A use case with increased risk exists in particular when
special categories of personal data within the meaning of Art. 9 GDPR are to be processed,
sensitive administrative, personnel, or application data is affected,
a permanent technical integration or automation (e.g., API-based further processing) is planned,
use takes place in the context of admission, examination, or personnel decisions, or
image data depicting persons is processed.
In these cases, approval by the responsible organizational unit with the involvement of the AI contact person is required before use; in the case of processing personal data, the involvement of the Data Protection Officer is additionally required.

evidence.quote:
2. Studies and Teaching
The use of Open WebUI in studies and teaching is permitted in accordance with §§ 4, 5 of the AI Directive. Specific permitted usage scenarios are regulated in Annex 1.
Automated assessment of examination performance and analysis of student behavior are not permitted. Examination decisions must always be made by a responsible natural person.
3. Administration
In central and decentralized university administration, Open WebUI may be used in a supportive capacity within the framework of § 6 of the AI Directive. Permitted uses include in particular:
Creating, revising, or translating texts,
Structuring information,
Analyzing documents,
Preparing decision bases, proposals, and concept papers,
Drafting emails,
Creating material-based chatbots,
as well as the usage scenarios regulated in Annex 1.
Decisions with legal effect must always be reviewed and ultimately assumed by a human entity (cf. § 6 para. 3 of the AI Directive).
IV. Processing of Personal and Confidential Data
The processing of personal data by Open WebUI is furthermore governed by § 7 of the AI Directive and the data protection regulations. Personal data may only be processed if a legal basis exists and the processing is limited to what is necessary. Input within the framework of the usage scenarios regulated in Annex 1 is generally permitted.
In use cases with increased risk, the use must be documented appropriately. Documentation is carried out by the respective responsible organizational unit with the involvement of the AI contact person. Information on internal processes, strategies, financial and personnel matters, IT security concepts, or contractually protected content may only be processed if this is professionally necessary and legally permissible.

evidence.quote:
V. Uploading Documents and Knowledge Databases (RAG)
Uploading documents to configure personal knowledge databases (Retrieval Augmented Generation – RAG) is permitted if the source materials may be used lawfully.
Uploaded files are technically processed and stored in a vector database. Automatic updating does not take place. Users are responsible for the currency and lawfulness of the stored content. Cross-departmental sharing of knowledge databases may only take place if a legal basis exists for this purpose.
VI. Use of External AI Models, API Usage, and Usage Volume
Open WebUI provides access to multiple Large Language Models (LLMs), including those from OpenAI (ChatGPT) or mistralAI, via an API. Inputs to third-party providers are processed according to their policies and may be stored temporarily. Your inputs are not used as training data. Chat content entered in Open WebUI does not become training data for the third-party LLMs. The use of Open WebUI is limited to the models approved by the University of Freiburg. Further model restrictions may apply to certain use cases. The provisions in Annex 1 are authoritative.
The use of the Open WebUI API is only permitted within the framework of approved projects, for study or teaching purposes, or as part of personal official use (e.g., programming environments) and in compliance with IT security requirements. Unauthorized connection of services that create a sustainable dependency or high automated usage load (e.g., batch processing) is not permitted. Please contact ki@rz.uni-freiburg.de for clarification.
Usage volume
To ensure fair and resource-efficient operation, a daily usage volume may be set for the use of Open WebUI. This may relate in particular to the number of requests, the processed token volume, or a monetary usage equivalent. If the set daily limit is reached, the following message appears: "You have reached your current daily request limit. If you need increased usage for a research project or for any other reason, please contact ki@rz.uni-freiburg.de." An adjustment of the individual usage volume is possible upon reasoned request. The decision is made within the framework of available technical and financial resources.
VII. Documentation of Usage Scenarios (Annex 1)
The specifically reviewed and approved usage scenarios of Open WebUI are documented in Annex 1. Annex 1 is maintained as a continuously updated document. Updates are carried out by the AI Commission. Changes and additions require approval by the Data Protection Officer and the Information Security Officer of the university.
Updates are announced in Open WebUI and are binding from the time of announcement.
VIII. Sustainability Guidelines
Users should be aware that the provision and use of generative AI models involve high energy consumption. Requests should only be made when necessary.

evidence.quote:
2. SCOPE
This policy applies to student and faculty use of generative AI and related AI-
enabled tools in connection with coursework, instruction, assessment,
academic research, AI-assisted feedback, and learning activities. It applies
to all schools, programs, courses, and instructional modalities unless a more
restrictive school, program, course, professional, accreditation, or legal
requirement applies.

   •   Coursework
   •   Instruction
   •   Assessment
   •   AI-assisted academic research
   •   AI-assisted feedback
   •   Generative AI tools used by students and instructors

This policy does not govern institutional research administration, human
resources, admissions, procurement, operational analytics, or other
administrative uses of AI that are governed by separate University policies or
procedures.

Clear expectations: Faculty should communicate permitted and prohibited
AI uses clearly in syllabi, assignment instructions, and other course materials.
Where course or assignment expectations are unclear, students are
responsible for seeking clarification before using AI.

evidence.quote:
6. FRAMEWORK FOR STUDENT USE OF AI
Faculty determine the appropriate level of AI use for their courses and
assignments based on learning outcomes, disciplinary expectations, and
pedagogical goals. The following framework provides a common University
structure for communicating those expectations to students and is intended
to support, rather than replace, faculty academic judgment.

Level 0
No AI use is permitted for the assignment or activity. Students may not use AI
to brainstorm, draft, revise, research, analyze, translate, summarize, solve,
code, edit, or otherwise assist with the submitted work unless the instructor
provides a specific written exception.

Level 1
AI may be used for limited preparatory support, including concept
clarification, study assistance, grammar correction, citation formatting, and
other non-substantive support functions. AI may not generate, draft, or
significantly shape submitted work unless the instructor expressly permits that
use for the assignment.

Guidance Note
Examples of permitted and non-permitted use include:

Permitted

   •   spelling correction
   •   grammar correction
   •   formatting
   •   citation formatting

Not Permitted

   •   generating paragraphs
   •   restructuring arguments
   •   rewriting substantive content
   •   producing analyses submitted as original work

C) Unsanctioned Use of Artificial Intelligence
Definitions: The fundamental principle guiding Yeshiva University’s Academic Integrity Policy is that all work submitted by students should be their own. Artificial Intelligence (AI) represents a tool that has the potential to be used either in accordance with this principle or in conflict with it. For the purposes of this policy, AI technologies are parsed into Generative AI and Assistive AI. It is the student’s responsibility to know what type of platform he/she is using, if use of that platform is allowed in his/her course, and, if so, for what purposes. Unsanctioned use of Generative AI or Assistive AI constitutes a potential academic integrity violation.
Generative AI is any AI platform that has the ability to create content from user inputs. Such platforms include but are not limited to: ChatGPT, Grok, CLAUD, Gemini, JASPER, Bard, DeepMind, DALL-E, Grammarly, etc. Because Generative AI can create content, it has significant potential to be used in ways that are inconsistent with the guiding principle of academic integrity. As such, students should be cautious. Students should assume that the use of any platform with generative capabilities is prohibited in their course, even if the platform is used for a non-generative purpose.
Faculty members may choose to allow the use of Generative AI in their courses or on particular assessments as they see fit. Those who allow the use of Generative AI should specify, in writing, how it may be used in the course and on specific assessments. It is up to the student to be aware of institutional and course policies regarding the use of Generative AI as well as policies pertaining to individual assessments. Content produced using Generative AI must be cited according to the conventions in the relevant subject area. Using any program not expressly sanctioned by the faculty member or using approved programs for any purpose other than those expressly authorized by the faculty member is a potential violation of academic integrity.
Assistive AI is any AI platform that aids the user in producing his/her own original content or refining the user’s original content without generating any substantive content itself. Examples of Assistive AI include, but are not limited to, Hemmingway, MS Editor, etc. Because such platforms do not create substantive content themselves, the use of Assistive AI is not assumed to represent a potential academic integrity violation. However, individual faculty members or departments may choose to limit or prohibit the use of Assistive AI in their courses or on particular assessments. Using any technology or assistance not expressly sanctioned by the faculty member or using approved technology or assistance for any purpose other than those expressly authorized by the faculty member, is a potential violation of academic integrity. It is the responsibility of the student to know what Assistive AI technologies are sanctioned by their instructors and the specific purposes for which their use is permitted.

evidence.quote:
A) For Unintentional Misuse of Sources
If a faculty member determines that a student unintentionally misused sources on an assignment or examination, he/she should report the incident to the AIC by submitting the Integrity Case Referral Form available on the academic integrity website, request that the matter be handled as a minor charge, and propose an appropriate penalty when submitting the Integrity Case Referral Form. The AIC may approve the request as is, suggest modifications to the proposed penalty, or deny the request.
Handling of a case as a minor charge does not involve a formal AIC hearing and only applies to minor infractions best treated as teachable moments. An infraction may only be handled as a minor charge if the student admits in writing to the infraction, and the AIC approves the request.
If the request to handle the infraction as a minor charge is approved by the AIC, the faculty member should provide guidance to the student on the issue that led to the charges (and notify the AIC after the guidance is provided) and should impose the penalty approved by the AIC, such as lowering the grade on the assignment (or examination) in question (including lowering to a grade of "F”). No additional penalty should be imposed.
The AIC will maintain a record of the incident and that the student has received instruction on proper practices. The incident will not be part of the student’s official permanent record at that time but will be used to inform whether leniency is appropriate should academic integrity issues arise with the student again in the future. evidence.quote:
General Expectations
All work submitted for assessment at the ANU Law School must be your own independent and original work. This means that you must not use generative AI to draft your assessment content.
The use of AI tools to support your learning is allowed in limited ways — for example, to help with expression, structure, or idea development — but not to generate your primary text.
Using AI inappropriately may breach the Academic Integrity Rule 2021 and, for law students, may also have serious consequences for admission to legal practice, as breaches must be disclosed to the relevant admissions authority.
You are at university to develop skills. This requires you to engage actively with assessment tasks rather than outsourcing your thinking and writing and requires you to draft and refine your own work. AI can help you polish your thinking, but it must not do the thinking for you.
Used appropriately, AI can be a useful tool to assist with editing and planning. However, it cannot be used to replace your reasoning, nor to write your work for you.
AI is best applied only to small portions of text. Submitting work generated in large part by AI increases the likelihood of poor-quality results and academic integrity concerns.
What Is Not Permitted
Using AI to generate whole or substantial sections of your assessment (e.g. essays, problem questions, theses, or oral presentations).
Relying on AI for research, legal reasoning, or case selection, without verification.
Composing your submission primarily or entirely with AI assistance.
Submitting AI-generated content without disclosure or passing off non-human output as your own.
What May Be Permitted (with Caution)
Using AI to improve expression in your own draft, such as grammar, clarity, or structure.
Prompting AI for ideas or to help brainstorm — provided you verify all information independently.
Being guided by your course convenor’s instructions, which may permit or restrict AI use in specific ways. Always check your assessment instructions carefully.
AI Is Not a Substitute for Research or Legal Reasoning
AI tools can suggest ideas or directions but are generally unreliable for legal research and problem-solving.
They are prone to hallucination, outdated information, and reliance on biased or non-verifiable data.
Legal analysis requires precision, citation of authoritative sources, and context — all of which require your judgement and legal training.
Principles for Appropriate Use of AI in Law
Originality: Any submitted work must be your own. AI must not be used to produce original content on your behalf.
Transparency: If you use AI, you must clearly declare it in your submission, including what tool you used, for what purpose, and how extensively.
Responsibility: You are responsible for the content you submit — including any factual, legal, or stylistic errors introduced by AI. Review all outputs carefully. You must understand and accept the declaration that accompanies all assessment submissions.
Accountability: Retain records of all prompts entered into AI tools and all outputs of those tools produced in the process of preparing for your assessment. These must be provided to any academic integrity processes on the convenor’s request.

evidence.quote:
Students retain Intellectual Property ownership of their assignments, even when they have been submitted for assessment. Therefore, staff are not permitted to upload student work to an AI platform without their express consent.
Can I upload University corporate data to AI software?
Even where data is de-identified, it remains a University asset. New uses of ANU data should be approved by the relevant data custodian, to ensure the use of the data is appropriate and that risks are adequately managed. The data custodian will depend on the type of data, but will typically be the Director/head of the local area that is responsible for the data.
I really need to use AI for my project. Can I just purchase my own software or use a free web-based tool?
All technical solutions being used for University business and/or on ANU managed devices must be approved by the University. This is to ensure appropriate data governance, information security and licencing. Freeware poses particular risks of inadequate information security controls and unapproved software puts the ANU network at risk. Staff must comply with the Acceptable use of information technology policy. Requests for AI software may be made to the ANU ServiceDesk.
Can I use AI to write or edit my emails or business documents?
It is important to ensure that you are not sharing any personal or corporate information with AI software, without the appropriate consents and approvals. Take care when asking AI to write or edit for University business and remember that AI has limitations. ANU staff should primarily be producing outputs required for University business. It is important for the University to be transparent about the way it makes and documents decisions. Remember that access to University documents can be requested under the Freedom of Information Act.

records.statement: Inappropriate uses of generative AI on any work submitted to fulfill an academic requirement constitute violations of academic integrity, such as directly copying the output, representing output generated by or derived from generative AI as one's own (including rewording or paraphrasing output from generative AI and representing it as one's own), exceeding the parameters of use specified by the instructor, or failing to disclose its use (including the use of generative AI for rewording, paraphrasing, or editing).

scope.audience: students

conditions: on any work submitted to fulfill an academic requirement

evidence.quote: Students are responsible for adhering to course and departmental policies regarding the use of generative AI. Inappropriate uses of generative AI on any work submitted to fulfill an academic requirement, such as directly copying the output, representing output generated by or derived from generative AI as their own (including rewording or paraphrasing output from generative AI and representing it as their own), exceeding the parameters of use specified by the instructor, or failing to disclose its use (including the use of generative AI for rewording, paraphrasing or editing) constitute violations of academic integrity.

### Generative AI

Generative AI is not a source as defined in this provision because its output is not created by a person. If generative AI is permitted by the instructor, students must _disclose_ its use rather than _cite_ or _acknowledge_ the use, since it is an algorithm rather than a source.

Students are responsible for adhering to course and departmental policies regarding the use of generative AI. Inappropriate uses of generative AI on any work submitted to fulfill an academic requirement, such as directly copying the output, representing output generated by or derived from generative AI as their own (including rewording or paraphrasing output from generative AI and representing it as their own), exceeding the parameters of use specified by the instructor, or failing to disclose its use (including the use of generative AI for rewording, paraphrasing or editing) constitute violations of academic integrity.

Jurisdiction over violations of academic rules and regulations rests with two distinct committees at Princeton. All in-class undergraduate written examinations and tests are conducted under the honor system. All violations of the honor system are the concern of the Undergraduate Honor Committee. Violations of rules and regulations pertaining to all other academic work, including essays, term papers, laboratory reports, and take-home and remotely taken examinations fall under the jurisdiction of the Faculty-Student Committee on Discipline. Should there be any uncertainty regarding which body is responsible for the adjudication of a particular case, clarification should be requested from the Office of the Dean of Undergraduate Students or the chair of the Honor Committee.

evidence.quote:
As [Rights, Rules, andResponsibilities Link is external](https://rrr.princeton.edu/students-and-university/24-academic-regulations) states:

> _As defined in section_ [_2.4.7 Link is external_](https://rrr.princeton.edu/students-and-university/24-academic-regulations#comp247) _, generative artificial intelligence (AI) is not a source, since its output is not produced by a person. If generative AI is permitted by the instructor (for brainstorming, outlining, etc.), students must disclose its use rather than cite or acknowledge the use, since it is an algorithm rather than a source._

All the tenets of scholarly integrity apply to use of generative AI: students must not pass off any output by generative AI as their own, and so a failure of disclosure, even in a course where generative AI is permitted, is a scholarly integrity violation. Check with your instructor about the disclosure template or use the template below.

A Template for Disclosing AI Usage

“This document was created with assistance from AI tools. Specifically, I used \[ _insert which AI tool_\] for \[ _insert purpose: brainstorming, outlining, generating content for sections of text on pages (insert pages), revising or proofreading text, formatting citations, etc._\]. I have reviewed and edited this work and have retained records of my generative AI use. For more information on the extent and nature of AI usage, please contact me.”

Be aware that different fields have different expectations for how to properly disclose—and in some disciplines, cite—generative AI. For example, the Modern Language Association expects you to provide much of the typical bibliographic information you would for a source and to provide a URL for accessing your conversation with the AI tool you used (which is possible if you’re logged into an account with ChatGPT or through browser extensions that enable link creation).

evidence.quote:
As a teacher, to what extent can I decide for myself which AI tools are permitted in my teaching and examinations and which are prohibited?
Unless specifically regulated by the faculty, responsibility lies with the course director. They can decide what is and what is not permitted in their course and at what time. In the case of courses with examinations, the use of AI could be permitted for certain work assignments, for example. In any case, students are responsible for any errors generated by AI (including missing citations).
In any case, clear and transparent communication with students is important. Students should also be able to talk about their previous experiences of using AI tools in their studies in courses and thus contribute to the discourse and an informed approach.
If students are asked to use AI in courses, care should be taken to ensure that the recommended tools are accessible and usable for everyone (free of charge).
I’m a student. How do I know whether the use of AI tools is permitted in a course?
Whether students are permitted to use generative AI tools in a course, and if so which ones, should be specified in the course description in the course catalogue before the course begins.
I’m a student. How do I know if I’m allowed to use KI-tools in an exam?
Permitted aids (including AI tools) in examinations must be explicitly stated by the course coordinator at the start of the course – ideally in the course catalogue before the course begins; any aids not mentioned are prohibited. Should unauthorised aids nevertheless be used, this shall be regarded as an attempt at cheating.
AI and research
Is it allowed to use AI tools?
Yes, of course, the general principles and standards of good scientific practice must be observed.
How should I label the use of AI tools?
When using AI tools, the guidelines for good scientific practice apply at the University of Innsbruck. The basic principles of transparency and traceability of the generated knowledge must also be ensured when using generative AI models. Therefore, any use of AI tools (name of the tool, scope of use, purpose of use) in the writing of scientific papers must be cited in the appropriate place. Texts, tables, images, videos, software codes, data sets, etc. generated by generative AI must be transparently identified. However, the AI source should not be cited as the author, as AI cannot be considered a scientific source and copyright issues arise.

evidence.quote:
Does the University of Innsbruck offer AI tools?
The University of Innsbruck offers its current staff a chatbot based on OpenAI technology, as well as a document analysis tool. The model runs in a secure environment and the data entered is not used for training purposes. The service is available at https://uibk.academic-ai.at/. Full details on how to use the service can be found on the website of the Department of Digital Media and Learning Technologies.
At the University of Innsbruck, the Microsoft 365 package includes the AI tool CoPilot, which cannot be technically disabled. As CoPilot is not part of the university’s overall package, there are no agreements with Microsoft regarding the protection of personal data. Among other things, data processing may take place outside Europe, and all input into CoPilot is used by Microsoft to train the model. For data protection reasons, all staff members are therefore expressly prohibited from using CoPilot.
Does the University of Innsbruck recommend the use of certain AI tools?
The University of Innsbruck recommends the use of the in-house AI model Academic AI. The model runs in a secure environment and the data entered is not used for training purposes. All information about the service can be found on the homepage of the eCampus of the e-learning department at the ZID.
You can find futher information on AI tools for teaching and research on this blogpost at the Crashkurs E-Didaktik in OLAT run by the e-learning department at the ZID (only available in German).
Who pays the licence fees for the use of fee-based AI products?
The University of Innsbruck makes the in-house modell Academic AI available to its employees free of charge with a credit of tokens worth €20 per month. Beyond this, there is no central assumption of costs for the use of other AI tools by the university. However, any license fees can be paid from institute, project or department budgets.

evidence.quote:
Who owns the output of AI generators?
Firstly, the output of a system does not give rise to a copyright for the system itself, as European copyright laws are based on a human act of creation, the realisation of which results in the creation of a work worthy of protection. An AI system is not human and therefore not a sufficient creator. In principle, the system manufacturer also does not establish any copyright in the system output, as it is not sufficiently creative in its creation process. Finally, the user may be entitled to a copyright in the output if they have merely used the AI system as a tool in their creative process. It is disputed whether this is already the case if the user selects a particularly creative prompt, or whether the user must also use the output, such as creating a collage from various AI-generated outputs.
What legal considerations do I need to bear in mind when using AI tools?
Personal data or copyright-protected data must not be entered into freely accessible AI tools; it is recommended that you use tools licensed by the University of Innsbruck that comply with data protection regulations, currently Academic AI.

evidence.quote:
Generative AI and Education: University of Waikato’s position
Most people are aware of the ongoing discussions around the use of Generative AI in education (GenAI). This page outlines the University of Waikato’s current stance and provides links to guidance we’ve developed to support students and staff.
In the Paper Outline Tool, accessible via Moodle and available to all learners, the following guidance explains what is permitted. However, if you're unsure, always check with your paper convener or lecturer.
Cheating at the University includes, but is not limited to:
Using an AI tool (e.g., ChatGPT) to generate your assignment or test answers and submitting them as your own, unless the assignment specifically requires the use of such a tool (does not apply to Studiosity, which is an approved AI tool).
Using an AI tool (e.g., ChatGPT) to rewrite your assignment or test answers and submitting them as your own, unless explicitly permitted in the assignment instructions (does not apply to Studiosity, which is an approved AI tool).
If you're interested in learning more about how AI can be used responsibly in your studies, refer to the library guide: How To Use GenAI/ChatGPT Responsibly: A Guide to Generative AI and Best Practices (opens in a new tab).
If you are unsure what constitutes academic misconduct, or plagiarism, enrol yourself into the new Academic Integrity Course in Moodle (opens in a new tab) and work through the tasks in your own time.
This module will highlight common types of academic misconduct including the risks associated with GenAI and guide you on how to avoid getting into trouble.

evidence.quote:
Provision for appeal to the Chairperson of the Academic Integrity Panel
Any party to a complaint of student misconduct (the complainant or the student who was the subject of the complaint) may appeal to the Chairperson of the Academic Integrity Panel against any decision taken by an Academic Integrity Representative or Associate Academic Integrity Representative under section 16 of these regulations
An appeal must be addressed and submitted in writing to the Chairperson of the Academic Integrity Panel, together with the prescribed fee.
An appeal must be received by the Chairperson of the Academic Integrity Panel not more than 14 days after the date on which the relevant decision was formally notified, and must include details of the grounds for the appeal.
An appeal may be made only on one or more of the following grounds:
that the process used for addressing the alleged misconduct was unfair
that the decision reached was manifestly at odds with the evidence
that the remedy imposed was manifestly at odds with the misconduct
that significant new evidence has become available that could not reasonably have been obtained and presented during the initial process and that could have a material effect on the outcome.
The Chairperson of the Academic Integrity Panel must hear the appeal as expeditiously as possible.
The appellant and the authority that made the original discipline decision
must be given the opportunity to appear and give evidence at the appeal hearing
may be accompanied by another person to act as an adviser or support person, subject to any conditions that the Chairperson of the Academic Integrity Panel may impose.
Having heard an appeal, the Chairperson of the Academic Integrity Panel may
dismiss the appeal and uphold the original decision
vary the decision with respect to the original complaint
require any appropriate and available remedy to settle the appeal.
The Chairperson of the Academic Integrity Panel may not impose a penalty that could not otherwise be imposed under these regulations by the authority that made the decision appealed against.
The outcome must be communicated to the appellant and the authority that made the original discipline decision as expeditiously as possible.
Failure to comply with a resolution negotiated or determined under this section is misconduct.
The decision of the Chairperson of the Academic Integrity Panel on an appeal is final.
At the discretion of the Chairperson of the Academic Integrity Panel, the fee for an appeal may be refunded, either in full or in part, if the appeal is decided in the appellant's favour.

evidence.evidenceSnippet:
Generative AI and Education: University of Waikato’s position
Most people are aware of the ongoing discussions around the use of Generative AI in education (GenAI). This page outlines the University of Waikato’s current stance and provides links to guidance we’ve developed to support students and staff.
In the Paper Outline Tool, accessible via Moodle and available to all learners, the following guidance explains what is permitted. However, if you're unsure, always check with your paper convener or lecturer.
Cheating at the University includes, but is not limited to:
Using an AI tool (e.g., ChatGPT) to generate your assignment or test answers and submitting them as your own, unless the

assignment specifically requires the use of such a tool (does not apply to Studiosity, which is an approved AI tool).
Using an AI tool (e.g., ChatGPT) to rewrite your assignment or test answers and submitting them as your own, unless explicitly permitted in the assignment instructions (does not apply to Studiosity, which is an approved AI tool).
If you're interested in learning more about how AI can be used responsibly in your studies, refer to the library guide: How To Use GenAI/ChatGPT Responsibly: A Guide to Generative AI and Best Practices (opens in a new tab).
If you are unsure what constitutes academic misconduct, or plagiarism, enrol yourself into the new Academic Integrity Course in

Moodle (opens in a new tab) and work through the tasks in your own time.
This module will highlight common types of academic misconduct including the risks associated with GenAI and guide you on how to avoid getting into trouble.

records.statement: CELT leaves the extent of student GenAI use to instructors, potentially assignment by assignment. The no-use, conditional-use and unrestricted-use statements on this page are examples for adoption, not simultaneous University rules. Citation, acknowledgement, prompts and percentage wording in an example apply only if the actual course adopts that condition.

scope.audience: Instructors choosing course policies; students following the policy actually adopted in their course
qualifiers: Only the captured source, version, audience and conditions; no exhaustive currency certification.

conditions: Follow the actual course and assignment policy; these are model statements rather than proof of course adoption.

evidence.quote:
It is up to the instructor to decide whether student use of generative AI (GenAI) is appropriate for their courses and to what extent. When making that decision, instructors should take into consideration the learning goals of the course, the content, and the extent to which that course can contribute to students' general experience and understanding of AI. For extensive, research-informed recommendations from UK ADVANCE, be sure to visit their website.
Instructors might also consider an assignment-by-assignment approach to identifying when generative AI is allowed. Consider using the Student AI Use scale as a possible resource for communicating specifically about what types of AI-augmented actions are appropriate and when at a course level or for each major assignments. Have conversations with students about your policy to offer transparency around disciplinary approaches to AI and to invite them to think critically about AI use.

Conditional Use
In some cases, instructors might want to help students explore GenAI in the context of their course and are, therefore, open to student use of AI in specified instances. CELT refers to these types of policies as “conditional AI use.” The exact policies outlining conditional use of AI vary widely based on learning goals and uses. For instance, instructors may choose to allow student use of AI:
for specified assignments only;
for specific stages or tasks in preparation for all assignments (i.e. brainstorming, proofreading, etc. but not drafting); or
for in-class activities only (not for completing individual or group assignments).
Instructors may also specify which GenAI tools students may or may not use. In most cases for assignment use, instructors should provide students with guidance about how to cite and acknowledge their use of AI. For instructors interested in considering possible ways to incorporate AI into their teaching, contact CELT for a consultation.
Example 1 - Use for Some Assignments
Students will be permitted to use GenAI tools for specific assignments only. When GenAI tools can be used on an assignment it will be explicitly stated in the directions. At times, instructions may also indicate the specific AI tool you can use. The goal of allowing the use of GenAI for these assignments is to make space for critical engagement and practice with these tools.
Students must cite any use of GenAI for any part of an assignment (from idea generation to text creation to text editing) using the guidelines from [insert name and link to relevant style guide]. Any use of AI beyond the assignments and tasks the instructor approves will be considered misuse. Also, failure to cite AI materials appropriately will be considered misuse and consequences will follow University policies.
Example 2 - Use for In-Class Activities Only
Students will be permitted to use Generative AI in this course only for specified tasks as designated by the instructor. Because Generative AI is an influential tool for the future of [insert discipline], it is important that students engage with that tool in thoughtful and inquisitive ways. As a result, there will be some specifically designed in-class activities where students are asked to use [insert GenAI tool name (i.e., ChatGPT, Bing, etc.)] to critically engage with its evolving abilities and restrictions. Please note that while we may use AI for some in-class activities, students may not use GenAI tools for any other assignment submissions.
Students who do not wish to sign up for [insert Gen AI tool] for in-class activities will be allowed to pair up with another student who has an account. Students are not required to give credit to AI tools for these activities as all students will be expected to use [insert tool name] in the same ways.
Misuse of AI in the context of this course includes submitting AI-generated outputs (in their original form or re-written) as your own work on class assignments. That type of misuse may be considered academic misconduct and consequences will follow University policies.
Example 3 - Specific Tasks Only & Acknowledgement
In this course you are permitted to use Generative AI for planning, organizing, outlining, brainstorming, and copy-editing your work for any major or minor assignment. However, you are not permitted to use GenAI for composition, writing, or content generation. In other words, the final product that you turn in should be at least 75% [or other %] your work.
This course invites students to use Generative AI in augmentative ways to encourage a healthy curiosity and skepticism about the tools and how they work. Students who use AI for their assignments must include the following statement at the end of the document/with references or works cited.
“I acknowledge my use of Generative AI in the preparation of this assignment in the form of [insert GenAI tool name]. The [GenAI tool name] was used in the following ways: [List and explain all uses including steps to clarify, fact-check, and cite]. Specifically, the AI-authored contributions to this submission include: [list specific contributions]. I take full responsibility for the accuracy of information informed by the AI tools I used."
Students should also include in-text citations of any AI-informed information using guidelines from [insert style guide].

records.statement: CELT recommends alternative arrangements for students who do not wish to register for or use AI even when a task requires it, such as group work or comparing search results. It says students should never be asked to enter personal/private information. Its no-use guidance also cautions that AI detectors are ineffective; this is instructional guidance, not proof that an individual detector flag is correct or an exhaustive misconduct evidence rule.

scope.audience: Instructors designing AI activities and students concerned about registration or privacy
qualifiers: Only the captured source, version, audience and conditions; no exhaustive currency certification.

evidence.quote:
If use of AI is allowed in the course, the policy should include specific instructions for how to cite and acknowledge that use if required. Explore the recommendations from your discipline's preferred style guide for suggestions. Consider asking students to include "Acknowledgement of Use" statements where appropriate. Recommended language for such statements can be found in the examples below.
Alternatives to AI Use
Questions about ethics and impact of AI use are still being negotiated and discovered. In addition, questions about data privacy remain unanswered at this time. With that in mind, instructors should make accommodations for students who wish not to register for or use those tools (even when required for an assignment). Some examples of alternatives might include allowing students to work in groups or allowing students to use search engines instead of AI and compare results. Given existing questions about privacy, students should never be asked to input personal or private information into a GenAI tool.

No Use
Instructors may decide that student use of Generative AI is detrimental to their ability to meet course learning objectives and, thus, opt for a “no AI use” policy. In such cases, the syllabus AI policy statement should include a rationale for that choice to encourage student compliance. It should also include a clear indication of what constitutes misuse and what steps will be taken if misuse occurs. Keep in mind, though, that AI detectors have been shown to be ineffective (read more about the limitations of AI detectors in the ADVANCE guidelines).

evidence.quote:
What privacy concerns arise in using generative AI in research?

Inputting any research data into a generative AI tool renders that data available in the AI tool
and its use. Accordingly, data privacy review is needed before any Protected Data (AR 10.7) is
entered into a generative AI tool (whether the tool is publicly available or not) to ensure that
the tool’s data privacy and security program complies with all applicable laws and university
guidelines. This process can be initiated by contacting the UK Information Technology Services
Governance, Risk and Compliance (GRC) team at GRC@uky.edu.

Generative AI tools that are public and available for use by anyone pose elevated risks to
privacy when entering research data, in particular protected health information (PHI), personal
identifying information or other personal information protected by law such as FERPA, and any
proprietary information.

Unless the UKHC InfoSec Data Sharing Committee has confirmed the AI tool is HIPAA compliant
and supports PHI input, do not put research data containing PHI into a generative AI tool or
other software. Additionally, other non-public or proprietary research data should not be placed
into an open-source AI tool without UK ITS GRC approval.

localSummary.zh: 存档2024年4月UK ADVANCE研究建议要求任何Protected Data输入GenAI前先隐私审查，无论公开工具与否。PHI除UKHC InfoSec Data Sharing Committee确认HIPAA合规及支持PHI外不得输入；其他非公开／专有研究资料未经ITS GRC批准不应进开源AI。后来的Copilot访问公告不自动免这些研究条件。

records.statement: UK ADVANCE keeps research-content accuracy with human authors and does not designate GenAI as an author. Reported research should disclose which tool, where and how it was used; journal rules vary, with model/date reporting described as best practice. Thesis/dissertation/comprehensive-exam use additionally depends on disciplinary, departmental, College/Graduate School and adviser conditions.

scope.unit: Research reporting and separately theses/dissertations/comprehensive exams
scope.audience: Researchers/authors; graduate students under the relevant thesis or examination rules
qualifiers: Only the captured source, version, audience and conditions; no exhaustive currency certification.

evidence.quote:
Who is responsible for content generated by AI?
Generative AI cannot be designated authorship as it cannot be held accountable for issues such
as research misconduct/plagiarism or intellectual property misuse. Researchers are responsible
for the content and accuracy of all aspects of their work. Human authors must take
responsibility for the content and the accuracy, factualness, or veracity of the data and analysis
presented in the research. Generative AI enables potential use in research but “it does not
excuse our judgment or accountability.”2


How should generative AI use be described in reported research
results?
Journals have different rules for reporting the use of generative AI in manuscripts. Generally,
journals, including those by the publishing houses of Taylor and Francis and Springer have
stated that input from AI must be detailed in the Materials and Methods section,
Acknowledgement section, or similar section for transparency. Any publication of reported
results should disclose the use of a generative AI tool, which tool, for what parts of the
publication and how it was used. Other best practices include indicating the specific language
model in addition to the generative AI tool, as well as the date(s) of use, e.g., “ChatGPT Plus,
GPT-4, 19-20 September 2023.”

Can generative AI be used for theses, dissertations, or
comprehensive exams?
The use of generative AI in theses, dissertations (and the research underlying them), and
comprehensive exams will differ by discipline in what is considered appropriate. Check with your
disciplinary authorities, organizations, funding agencies, and publications for a more context-
specific understanding of how generative AI may be used in ways that are referenced,
disclosed, and/or cited appropriately. Additionally, make sure to consult all requirements,
guidelines, and regulations for theses, dissertations, and comprehensive exams (e.g., in the
department, college, and Graduate School), as well as the student’s chair or adviser.

evidence.quote:
These appeal procedures apply whenever a formal hearing has reached a decision for
an alleged violation of Academic Code.

B.    Grounds for Appeal

Any respondent who has been found responsible by a hearing panel may appeal either
the finding of responsibility, the sanction imposed or both.

The University may not appeal.

C.    The Notice of Appeal

A respondent may appeal by filing a notice of appeal with the Academic Ombud
within seven (7) business days of the decision determining the sanction.

The notice must state (a) the grounds of the appeal, and (b) whether the respondent
is appealing the finding of responsibility, the sanction imposed or both. Appeals not
filed in a timely manner will not be accepted or considered.

The Academic Appeals Panel hears the following types of appeals:
a final grade, dismissal, or different University decision (students have 90 days to contact the Academic Ombud to appeal to the Academic Appeals Panel);
an academic offense determination imposing a penalty of zero on the assignment or failure in the course (students have 10 days to contact the Academic to appeal to the Academic Appeals Panel).
a decision by the Academic Hearing Panel (students have 7 days to contact the Academic Ombud to appeal the Academic Hearing Panel's decision).
Academic Hearing Panel
A formal hearing by the Academic Hearing Panel is required:
if the penalty to be imposed is harsher than failure in a course. A hearing panel will be convened to review the evidence to determine if an offense occurred, and if so, the proper penalty to be applied.
if a student is found responsible by the Academic Hearing Panel, the student may appeal their decision to the Academic Appeals Panel by filing a notice of appeal with the Academic Ombud within seven (7) business days of the Academic Hearing Panel's decision.

don't leave your assignments around for others to read

4.1 Data Classification
All AI usage must align with Swinburne’s Data Classification and Privacy Frameworks:
Public Data: Can be shared into any AI system, provided such use is in line with other applicable laws, frameworks, and policies for such uses (e.g. copyright)
Internal Data: Only use with enterprise AI tools.
Sensitive or Restricted Data: Must not be entered into any AI system which does not have enterprise data protection. This includes, but is not limited to:
personally Identifiable Information (PII), as defined pursuant to section 3 of the Privacy & Data Protection Act 2014 (Vic)
health information, as defined pursuant to section 3 of the Health Records Act (Vic)
student records
staff details

evidence.quote:
14. Application for review of a decision
1. A person may apply for review of a decision if
a. the decision was a reviewable decision affecting the person in his or her capacity as a student; and
b. unless accepted under regulation 15, the application is made within 21 working days after
i. the student has been notified of the decision; or
ii. the deemed refusal.
2. An application for review of a decision must
a. be made in writing in the form set out in Schedule 1;
b. specify the grounds on which the applicant relies; and
c. be lodged with the Registrar.
15. Acceptance of application by Registrar
1. The Registrar may accept a late application for review of a decision, taking into consideration
a. how late the application is;
b. the reasons why it is late; and
c. whether the delay has caused prejudice or will have an adverse effect on University administration.

Can I apply for a review?
You can apply for a review of a University decision if:
you apply within 21 working days of receiving notice of the decision
the decision is 'reviewable'.
'Reviewable' decisions
A decision will be 'reviewable' if it falls under one of the following categories:
Type of 'reviewable' decision
Description
Example
General misconduct decision
A decision made about the general misconduct of a student under University regulations.

A decision made about the academic misconduct of a student under University regulations.

18. Grounds for appeal
1. A person may apply to the University Secretary to appeal the decision of a review officer.

a. that there is relevant evidence that—
i. was not taken into consideration by the review officer; and
ii. which could not have been known by the person prior to the review;

a. in writing in the form set out in Schedule 2;

a. how late the application is;

evidence.quote:
Integrity and purposeful use
Users must ensure AI-generated content complies with Swinburne’s intellectual property and academic integrity policies and regulations.
Users must respect intellectual property laws, including Indigenous cultural and intellectual property considerations, and creators’ moral rights of attribution and integrity.
Users must ensure AI use is appropriately referenced in accordance with university referencing conventions.
Transparency and accountability
Users may use AI to assist decision-making but not as the sole authority in critical decisions, such as student grading, admissions, and hiring.
Fairness and accuracy
Users must assess AI-generated outputs for bias, particularly in hiring, admissions, research, and policymaking.
Users must apply human oversight when using AI tools for decision-making, ensuring AI recommendations are reviewed before implementation.
Privacy and data protection
Users must use AI in accordance with Swinburne’s Data Classification and Privacy Frameworks.
Users must ensure compliance with Swinburne’s data security, ethics, integrity and sovereignty requirements when using AI as part of an external collaboration. AI partnerships should be reviewed for risks related to intellectual property, data sharing, and regulatory compliance and as a result a Privacy Impact Assessment (PIA), Third Party Risk Assessment (TPRA) and Security Risk Assessment (SRA) need to be conducted.
Users must ensure compliance with Australian Research Council and National Health and Medical Research Council, funder and publisher policies on the use of AI in grant applications, peer review and authorship.

records.statement: Alberta student guidance states that the instructor submits a report to the Dean, who will consider the information, offer the student an opportunity to respond and decide between NDAO and the complaint process. NDAO requires Dean and student agreement. A Dean's choice not to offer NDAO is not appealable, but students may choose the complaint process.

scope.audience: students

evidence.quote:
Most cases of academic misconduct are resolved at the faculty level. Anyone can raise an academic integrity concern by bringing it to the attention of an instructor. The instructor may raise an academic integrity concern with the student and make any inquiries about the concern that they deem appropriate.

The instructor submits a report to the faculty dean. Upon receiving an academic integrity concern, the dean will consider the information and offer the student an opportunity to respond. The dean will consider the information and determine whether the matter should be addressed through non-disciplinary accountability options (NDAO) or a complaint process.

Both the dean and the student must agree that the NDAO process is the appropriate choice. If a dean declines to use an NDAO, there is no appeal for that decision. Students also have the right to engage in the complaint process and may choose to pursue it over the NDAO process.

### Overview

The [Student Academic Integrity Policy (SAIP)](https://www.ualberta.ca/en/alfresco/uappol/academic/student-academic-integrity/policy/student-academic-integrity-policy.pdf) is a formal policy that applies to all students at the university. This includes every individual who is registered in courses, is currently attending or has graduated from the university. It provides information on why the policy is in place and the university’s approach to academic misconduct.

This guide provides an overview of SAIP. If ever there is a discrepancy between the information provided here and the policy, the policy will be deemed accurate.

records.statement: NDAO requires the student to agree misconduct occurred and help determine measures. Its record is purged at graduation only after completing NDAO and never again being found responsible for academic misconduct; the claimed clean disciplinary record is qualified to SAIP.

evidence.quote:
### Non-disciplinary accountability options

NDAOs are agreements that faculties reach with students to hold them accountable for their behaviour and lay out a set of expectations on things the student will do and will not do in the future. The student has to agree that they have done something wrong and participate in determining appropriate ways of addressing it.

If a student completes the NDAO and is never again found to engage in academic misconduct, when they graduate the record of the NDAO will be purged and the student will be able to apply to other programs and legitimately say they have never been found to have violated a discipline policy, at least as far as SAIP is concerned.

This includes every individual who is registered in courses, is currently attending or has graduated from the university. It provides information on why the policy is in place and the university’s approach to academic misconduct.

This guide provides an overview of SAIP. If ever there is a discrepancy between the information provided here and the policy, the policy will be deemed accurate.

records.statement: In the complaint process a Dean-appointed Faculty Decision-Maker investigates and offers a hearing. Specific outcomes such as suspension, expulsion or degree suspension/revocation may be referred to Student Conduct and Accountability, rather than inferred as that officer’s direct powers.

scope.audience: students

evidence.quote:
### Complaint process

There are times when the behaviour addressed by the SAIP is simply too serious to be allowed to continue. If the faculty does not feel that a student is a candidate for a NDAO, or it is not possible to reach an agreement with the student, then the matter has to be referred to a faculty member to make a decision as to whether the student violated the policy and determine appropriate sanctions.

When a decision is made to address an academic integrity concern through the complaint process, the dean will assign a Faculty Decision-Maker. The Faculty Decision-Maker will offer the student a hearing and complete any necessary investigation to determine if the student is in violation of the Student Academic Integrity Policy.

Where the Faculty Decision-Maker determines that the student has violated the Student Academic Integrity Policy, they may impose one or more of the sanctions set out in [Schedule B](https://www.ualberta.ca/en/alfresco/uappol/academic/student-academic-integrity/appendix/student-academic-integrity-policy-appendix-b-sanction-descriptions-and-impact.pdf) of the Student Academic Integrity Policy. These may include: academic integrity conditions, grade sanctions, rescission of an admission offer or refusal to consider an application.

In some instances, a Faculty Decision-Maker may refer a case to Student Conduct and Accountability, where they seek to apply specific sanctions, such as suspension, expulsion, suspension of a degree and rescission of a degree.

## Support for students facing an allegation

Support is available for students facing allegations of academic misconduct. The [Office of the Student Ombuds](https://www.ualberta.ca/en/current-students/ombuds/services.html) can assist students in navigating the Student Academic Misconduct Process.

| Advisor | An individual who assists an appellant or respondent during the appeal process. Assistance may be provided by the Office of the Student Ombuds,Student Legal Services,legal counsel or another advisor chosen by the parties. |

### Overview

The [Student Academic Integrity Policy (SAIP)](https://www.ualberta.ca/en/alfresco/uappol/academic/student-academic-integrity/policy/student-academic-integrity-policy.pdf) is a formal policy that applies to all students at the university. This includes every individual who is registered in courses, is currently attending or has graduated from the university. It provides information on why the policy is in place and the university’s approach to academic misconduct.

This guide provides an overview of SAIP. If ever there is a discrepancy between the information provided here and the policy, the policy will be deemed accurate.

evidence.quote:
Each instructor, program and even assignment may have different rules on the use of artificial intelligence. For instance, it may be appropriate to use artificial intelligence to help build ideas on a topic for a research paper while it is inappropriate to use it to write the entire paper.
However, there are ways for students to better understand when its use is appropriate. The following tips can help students navigate the use of artificial intelligence in their coursework. Be proactive and follow these tips before you begin work in any of your courses.
Things to do
Read instructions and course syllabi
Every course offered by the university comes with a syllabus. A syllabus provides information on the course, assignments, and what is expected of students. Begin by carefully reading each of the course syllabi provided to you and find out if your instructor has outlined the use of artificial intelligence in their class.
Understand expectations
Understand what is expected of you for each and every assignment. A course syllabus is a great place to start understanding if the use of artificial intelligence is acceptable in your course. However, it is important to know exactly when and how you may use it. Check the details provided by your instructor on each and every assignment you are required to complete to ensure that you know if and how it is appropriate to use artificial intelligence on an assignment before you submit it.
Ask for clarification
Ask your instructor about when and how you may use artificial intelligence if you are unsure. It is a good idea to ask your instructor in writing so that you have a record to refer back to when completing your assignment.

evidence.quote:
Expansion of Gemini Tools for Faculty and Staff
2 February 2026
Following recent updates to Google for Education’s core services, the University of Alberta is preparing for an immediate rollout of several new AI features within our Google Workspace environment. These tools are being integrated as core services, ensuring they meet our institutional standards for data privacy and security. At this time, these new features will be implemented for faculty and staff only.
The following tools are expected to appear in your Workspace interface as of February 4, 2026.
Google Docs: Access "Help Me Write" for drafting technical documentation, grant summaries, or course descriptions. The side panel can also be used to summarize long-form documents or suggest structural changes.
Google Slides: Generate original visual aids and diagrams from text prompts directly within the presentation interface to assist with lecture delivery.
Google Forms: Use AI to generate draft assessment questions or surveys from a brief topic description. It also provides automated summaries of collected response data.
In the coming months, Google will implement Gemini functionality within Sheets and Gmail.
No manual installation is required; the Gemini icon will appear in the side panel of the respective apps once the update is live. Individual users cannot disable Gemini integrations in these applications.
Data Privacy and Security
The Gemini app is a core Google Workspace service supported by Information Services and Technology (IST) and is therefore included and protected by the University of Alberta’s agreement with Google. Google does not use University of Alberta data, prompts, or generated content to train its public AI models. All intellectual property remains within the university's controlled environment.
Gemini app activity from the web or mobile app cannot be deleted or turned off for Google Workspace for Education accounts (including for the University of Alberta). If you use the Gemini web or mobile app with a U of A account, your activity is turned on, and your conversation history is retained for 18 months. If you do not use Gemini, no data will be shared.
For more information on using Gemini, including details on information privacy best practices, visit the Get Started with Gemini article.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools like Gemini, ChatGPT, and Claude can be powerful resources, but it is important to understand how these tools use your data so you can make an informed decision about which tool may be most appropriate for your data.
This document is designed to help you determine what data can be safely shared with AI while ensuring compliance with the University of Alberta’s Information Security policies. It provides recommendations for safe data sharing based on four data categories: Restricted, Confidential, Protected, and Unrestricted. If you are unsure about how to classify your data, please contact Enterprise Information Governance.
This guide offers general recommendations on data safety when using AI tools, but it is not exhaustive. As AI technologies, privacy policies, and terms of use continue to evolve, it is your responsibility to assess whether sharing specific data is appropriate and secure. If you are unsure, follow the Information Security Policies or contact aiguide@ualberta.ca before proceeding.
Why we recommend Gemini
Google’s Gemini App provides an institutionally-approved, free and secure tool to respond to the demand for access to generative AI as a productivity tool. Interactions with the Gemini App stay within the Google Workspace Cloud isolated to the U of A and are not reviewed by humans or otherwise used to improve Google's generative AI models.
The Gemini App is currently the only generative AI platform that has been approved for use with University of Alberta data. While it is recommended as a safe generative AI option, in terms of data privacy and security, there are still limitations on what data is safe to use.
The table below provides more details on what types of data are safe to use with various types of data policies that AI tools commonly have. Other generative AI tools are not currently authorized for use involving University data and should be approached with caution.
If you are using AI tools for research, please connect with the Safeguarding Research Office (safegrd@ualberta.ca) to discuss the security considerations relating to use of AI tools to support your research.

Why can’t I access enhanced Gemini functionality like Gems or Gemini in Gmail and other Google Workspace for Education core services?
Gemini functionality such as Google Workspace core services integration or extensions (e.g., Gmail, Drive, and others) are not currently available for U of A accounts*. Additional limitations may also apply.
*The university is currently evaluating the paid enhanced versions of Gemini to understand what additional benefits it offers and where those benefits should be deployed given the cost associated with doing so.
Are my Gemini conversations reviewed by Google or used to train Google AI models?
No. The Gemini app is a core Google Workspace service supported by Information Services and Technology (IST) and is therefore included and protected by the University of Alberta’s agreement with Google. Interactions with the Gemini app stay within the University of Alberta and they are not reviewed by humans or otherwise used to improve Google's generative AI models.
How do I turn off or delete my Gemini app activity?
Gemini app conversation activity from the web or mobile app cannot be deleted or turned off for Google Workspace for Education accounts (including for the University of Alberta). If you use the Gemini web or mobile app with a U of A account, your activity is turned on and your conversation history is retained for 18 months.
What do I need to consider when submitting information to the Gemini App?
U of A Google Workspace is approved for storing and sharing the university's business, academic, research and administrative information and records. Extremely sensitive information such as identifiable patient and health care information, social insurance numbers and passport information, is not to be stored in or shared through U of A Google Workspace applications, including Gemini.

a.​ A student has the right to appeal the Faculty Decision-Maker's and, where applicable, the
             Student Conduct Officer's discipline decisions made under the Student Academic
             Misconduct Procedure. Appeals may not be submitted until after the final disciplinary
             decision has been made by either the Faculty Decision-Maker or the Student Conduct
             Officer. Where a discipline decision has been made by the Faculty Decision-Maker and
             not referred to the Student Conduct Officer, the student must submit an appeal within 15
             working days of the deemed receipt of the Faculty Decision-Maker’s decision. Should a
             decision by the Faculty Decision-Maker be referred to the Student Conduct Officer, the
             appeal of the Faculty Decision-Maker’s decision will be delayed until the Student Conduct
             Officer has completed their decision and both decisions will be subject to appeal at the
             same time.

         b.​ Both the Faculty and the student have a right to appeal the final decision of the Student
             Conduct Officer.

         c.​ All appeals to the Appeal Panel must be submitted within 15 working days of the deemed
             receipt of the relevant decision. Where the student has appealed a decision, the Faculty
             Decision-Maker who made the original decision will act in response for appeals of both
             their and the Student Conduct Officer’s decisions.

2.​ INITIATING AN APPEAL

c.​ Non-disciplinary accountability options are voluntary. As a result, where a student
          disagrees with the actions and/or assignments determined by the Dean, the student may
          opt to have the academic integrity concern addressed in a complaint. In that case, the
          Dean will follow the procedures under section 6.

      d.​ Where the Dean’s proposed actions and/or assignments would require the participation
          of any university service unit, office or individual, the Dean will ensure those university
          units, offices or individuals agree to participate before confirming those actions and/or
          assignments in writing.

      e.​ Where the student and the Dean agree, the actions and/or assignments and their
          agreement to them will be confirmed in writing. The actions and/or assignments must
          be specific and measurable and a date for their completion must be specified in the
          agreement. The actions and/or assignments should not involve the instructor who raised
          the academic integrity concern without the instructor’s consent.

      f.​ The Dean will monitor the student’s performance of the actions and/or assignments and,
          where appropriate, may, in writing, agree to extend any timelines or vary the actions
          and/or assignments set out in the agreement.

      g.​ The Dean will determine whether and when the student has successfully completed the
          actions and/or assignments by the timelines in their agreement. If the student disagrees
          with the Dean’s determinations in any of these respects, the student may, within 5
          working days of the decision, apply to a Student Conduct Officer for a decision on
          whether or not the terms of the agreement have been met. The Student Conduct Officer’s
          decision is final.

9.​ RECORDS

            a.​ The student’s academic integrity history will be kept in accordance with the applicable
                records retention procedures. Any record of completed expectations as laid out in a
                non-disciplinary accountability option will be expunged upon completion of the student’s
                academic program or upon the normal date of file destruction, whichever comes first.

NDAOs are agreements that faculties reach with students to hold them accountable for their behaviour and lay out a set of expectations on things the student will do and will not do in the future. The student has to agree that they have done something wrong and participate in determining appropriate ways of addressing it.
If a student completes the NDAO and is never again found to engage in academic misconduct, when they graduate the record of the NDAO will be purged and the student will be able to apply to other programs and legitimately say they have never been found to have violated a discipline policy, at least as far as SAIP is concerned.
Complaint process
There are times when the behaviour addressed by the SAIP is simply too serious to be allowed to continue. If the faculty does not feel that a student is a candidate for a NDAO, or it is not possible to reach an agreement with the student, then the matter has to be referred to a faculty member to make a decision as to whether the student violated the policy and determine appropriate sanctions.
When a decision is made to address an academic integrity concern through the complaint process, the dean will assign a Faculty Decision-Maker. The Faculty Decision-Maker will offer the student a hearing and complete any necessary investigation to determine if the student is in violation of the Student Academic Integrity Policy.
Where the Faculty Decision-Maker determines that the student has violated the Student Academic Integrity Policy, they may impose one or more of the sanctions set out in Schedule B of the Student Academic Integrity Policy. These may include: academic integrity conditions, grade sanctions, rescission of an admission offer or refusal to consider an application.
In some instances, a Faculty Decision-Maker may refer a case to Student Conduct and Accountability, where they seek to apply specific sanctions, such as suspension, expulsion, suspension of a degree and rescission of a degree.
Support for students facing an allegation
Support is available for students facing allegations of academic misconduct. The Office of the Student Ombuds can assist students in navigating the Student Academic Misconduct Process.
Student Academic Integrity Policy
Overview
The Student Academic Integrity Policy (SAIP) is a formal policy that applies to all students at the university. This includes every individual who is registered in courses, is currently attending or has graduated from the university. It provides information on why the policy is in place and the university’s approach to academic misconduct.
This guide provides an overview of SAIP. If ever there is a discrepancy between the information provided here and the policy, the policy will be deemed accurate.

Advisor                               An individual who assists an appellant or respondent during the
